Jun.title: Swimming Lessons
Jun.author: Claire Fuller
Jun.review:
“It’s difficult to live with both hope and grief.”

I have to admit that this sort of book and writing style will not appeal or suit to everyone. I had to put it down and pick it up several times to peak any sort of interest but Ingrid's letters got me hooked on what went wrong.
The book is a character-driven novel about love leading to marriage that ultimately was in ruins. Flora and her father are living in the hope that Ingrid would come back while Nan has a more realistic response to the situation and has taken up her mother's place in all the twelve years of disappearance.

The book in itself was alright in the least. We never really explore the emotional aspects hiding within the story even with the use of several metaphors. With that being said, the characters never really grew for me. There were no major developments in their personality aside from the slow realization that Flora's memories were heavily clouded and her realizing that her dad wasn't quite what she made him out to be.

The letters were enjoyable. The transition of Gil being this charming professor to a compulsive cheater was what struck out for me. I kind of understood why Ingrid never left the relationship since she held on to the hope that they were okay and would overcome this. But after their marriage, they had no connection to speak of. Ingrid didn't want children but she couldn't have used birth control? She gave up so much for someone whom she didn't have an emotional connection to. They never really talked even when Ingrid lost a child . He never really was there for her and used her for acquiring a story he never could have thought of by himself.
The only thing I really felt for this book was intrigue to what happened with Ingrid and anger at her misfortune and Gil's acts.

All books are created by the reader
I really liked the concept behind the running theme of how each reader interprets the book differently. The book left me with a strong message - no two readers read the same book. They define the plot and characters based on what they understand and draw from their experiences.

She is an alcoholic who doesn't have a job but lies about having one and then suddenly, on a night, she becomes involved with Jess and Jason's life and everything is not what it seems - much to her disappointment. She forgot what happened except the fact that Megan(Jess) is disappeared and she's one of the main suspects.
To prove her innocence and have something to pass her time with,she starts her personal investigation which leads to secrets being revealed and a banging finale.

I am sure that many of us already guessed who was the killer , early on, but Hawkins distracts the readers with further characterization and trivial sub-plots to focus on.

Despite some flaws, the book makes up to be an interesting read.

May.title: A Good Girl's Guide to Murder (A Good Girl's Guide to Murder, #1)
May.author: Holly  Jackson
May.review:
You know the feeling when the book you're reading engulfs you in a warm hug,makes you a part of its world and every character feels like an old friend you know? This was that book for me.
"A Good Girl's Guide to Murder" felt like home.With the old town setting & the sneaking around Pippa did, I was bombarded with memories of being a young kid and reading Famous Five/Nancy Drew.

Initially,I felt myself grumbling about the details given to the monotony of her life after every production log but as I read,I came to really appreciate the focus given to building Pippa's life beyond just the mystery. I've come to expect every character to have a life so intricate and complex because of the books I've read aimed as dark mystery however, this was an eye-opener to the fact that most young adults (such as myself) have had sheltered lives that revolve around books,universities and perhaps the occasional murder-mystery EPQ.

I loved the breakdown of this perfect little town into a town clouded with well-kept secrets lurking under the surface . Most characters,for me,were in the grey zone hanging between the right and the wrong due to their actions,motives and ultimately,the chain reaction that their actions started off.

The use of mixed media made the book highly interactive and I found myself constantly connecting different suspects for the likelihood of our double murder duo

If I had to pick,I'd take the speech Pippa gives in the very last chapter as the perfect end to a tumultuous ride.It highlighted so many things - not only about the victim but also of those involved - in the sense that most cases shell out everyone as one-dimensional but there are so many layers to each of them and I am happy that it was explored bit-by-bit as it was in this book and not all at once. The revelation bought on by all the pieces clicking at the very end was the cherry.
To be honest,I've just finished the book and I expect to write a better review but as of now,my heart is just so full that I finally read a book that got me clapping and screaming at my screen.
P.S - I just saw it's set to be a series so now I know what is going to be my next buy.

Sep.title: Blood Orange
Sep.author: Harriet Tyce
Sep.review:
Slight spoilers ahead

Upon initially finishing the book, my mind was set on this being a 4.5-stars - mainly because the climax of the plot was satisfying and every character got an arc that felt rightfully deserved. However, the more time I've had to process the character development and the plot itself, it bought the book down to a 2.5-stars.

The first half of the book seems to be in an infinite loop of Alison's mistakes, guilt and her toxic relationship with her husband. It is of no question that the author repeated the same scenario in different settings to emphasize the lack of both Alison's control over alcohol and the slow deterioration of her relationship with her husband. But it could have been done in so many ways. After a point, it was just the author reusing the same plot that she had typed for a good chunk of the book. With no character development to be seen in sight, it felt more like a "Oh shit, here we go again".

The synopsis sells itself as a struggling alcoholic whose anchor of hope turns out to be a client suspected of stabbing her husband. The book doesn't delve further into the murder, having taken a sideline when compared to the car-wreck that is Alison's life.

To top it all off, the threatening texts Alison receives only deters her for a chapter or two, where she decides that she will be more present in her daughter's life only for her to go back to Patrick and repeat her mistakes on a grander scale than before.

The reader is led to believe that her life is moving in a positive upward trajectory (so much so you can almost forget how terrible Carl is) only for it to be a red herring.

To the book's credit, the last 70 pages made up for the mess in the first half. Each chapter bought forth surprising revelations that alter every character's lives significantly and brings closure to several subplots. The multitude of smaller dramas along the way left me with disbelief at being misled by them.

Overall, there was a huge disjoint in my perception of what the book would be as opposed to what it was. The synopsis painted it as a story containing three over-arching subplots, however, only one of them was fleshed out properly, leading to slippery, poorly framed plots for the other two.

P.S. - were we supposed to believe Alison is good at her job? It was explicitly told to the reader quite a few times, however, just as the rule of "show, don't tell" goes, there was no evidence to back it up.

Sep.title: The Silent Patient
Sep.author: Alex Michaelides
Sep.review:
Slight Spoilers ahead! Alludes to the ending of the book quite a bit

Would you label me a novice if I said I did not see the ending of "The Silent Patient" coming? At the ungodly hour of 3 am, when I was definitely supposed to be asleep, I shifted from one side to another in apprehension after reading and re-reading the big twist. Would you label me an amateur if the intricacies of the psychology behind the one responsible for seeking the victim didn't dawn on me until it was laid out in layman's terms?


To be honest, I was fairly surprised by how much I liked this book. Despite the looming warning of an early start to the day, I ended up finishing the book in one sitting, driven by the thrill of Kathy's betrayal and Alicia's silence.

The impact of "The Silent Patient" does not come from a fast-paced mystery with twists at every turn, but in the quiet surprises Michaelides sneaks in each page. Michaelides builds the characters from 2-dimensional people, easily categorizable as fundamentally good or bad, to 3-dimensional complex people with motives behind each action stemming from their past. "The Silent Patient" shone, particularly, as a riveting character study of both Alicia and Theo, taking its time to reveal us the layers of each character one by one, leading the reader to second-guess their interpretations of what had happened.


Much like the title, the entire book is silent, depending on non-verbal cues via actions and thoughts of our characters as opposed to dialogues for framing the plot. This book is a demonstration of how easy it is to lie to yourself, but your actions will always be a dead giveaway to your deeds. (My apologies, I realize this sentence appears preachy and pretentious)

The author frames the central mystery around Alicia's self-portrait, painted after the murder of her husband, where she depicts herself as Alcestis, giving way to the question about what transpired the night of Gabriel's murder and why was it akin to Alcestis. Having taken upon the role of Alcestis after her husband's death, Alicia has shrouded herself in silence for the past six years and Theo, our protagonist, is of the belief that he can get her to communicate.

Hidden amongst the sessions and the bits of past of our main characters, we are introduced to the concept of countertransference, in which a therapist becomes emotionally untangled with his patient. Several dialogues and actions alluded to the fast decline of Theo's objectivity regarding Alicia, going above and beyond to put together snippets of Alicia's past, forcing the question to rise - Why?

Could Theo be transferring his feelings of unrequited love onto Alicia? Is Theo actively ignoring the distress in his own life by actively pursuing the truth behind Alicia? Or is there something else at play?

The blurred lines between the roles of therapist and patient hint that Theo and Alicia were linked. Perhaps they are even culpable for the same murder; co-actors in a tragedy akin to Alcestis.



With that being said, the book didn't hit all the spots for me. Several subplots were used as red herrings to distract the reader from the original culprit. However, they were poorly handled with many never being explored again or explained in a way that aligned the motives of those characters.

The psychiatric institution follows procedures unheard of in real life, painting everyone just a little "mad" because of their own line of work to excuse actions that would not be looked over. Had the author researched further the functioning of such an institute, especially in the setting he aimed to use it in, this book would have been a 5-star.
The very last thing that I would add is the emphasis on accents. Every time the reader was introduced to a new character who wasn't originally from the UK, there was always a bit about the character's accent via dialogues or Theo's POV. While trivial, this kind of annoyed me because there seemed no explicit need of it.

May.title: The Henna Artist (The Jaipur Trilogy, #1)
May.author: Alka Joshi
May.review:
The year is 1955. Cyclists, street vendors and nimble-footed pedestrians bustle about the dusty roads of Jaipur. Amidst it all, huddled inside a tonga beside her faithful helper and a litany of tiffins, is thirty-year-old Lakshmi Shastri: the henna artist working for Jaipur’s elite complete with flashbacks detailing her failed marriage, her parents and the ayurvedic teachings of her mother-in-law.
Lakshmi plays her role as the protagonist with grace, subverting expectations at every turn, navigating the landscapes of caste, class and patriarchal standards brimming under Jaipur’s luxurious pretences. On the other end of this spectrum is Radha, impatient, hard-headed and the kind of character one can’t help but roll their eyes at.Yet despite these traits, Radha shows moments of incredible strength and maturity, making it easy to forget that she is only a thirteen-year-old girl, and that like Lakshmi, she, too, has been a victim of society, circumstances, and the consequences of Lakshmi’s own actions from thirteen years ago.

In Alka Joshi’s debut novel, The Henna Artist, India is not just a country but an emotion embodied by the people who live there. At its core, this book is a tale of both individual and collective independence in a post-colonial India stuck between the richness of its culture and the allure of foreign trends. From distinguished ladies to battered servants, to hungry entrepreneurs like Lakshmi, this story is of women who dared to dream, to survive, and reach for a future beyond the bounds of their perceived station. At times a coming-of-age story, at times family drama, much like Lakshmi’s designs, its intricacies are deftly wrapped within the folds of time, place, and a deceptively simple narrative. It is also a subtle critique of India’s ancient caste system and its intersections with latter-day capitalism; of cerebral and financial equality in a world where women cannot so much as walk the streets without a husband or chaperone in tow -- a thing that is, in many ways, not so far removed from present-day India.

Alka Joshi worked on The Henna Artist for a decade before it was picked up for publication. The heart and soul she put into this novel shows – a story of hope, ambition and healing.

Jun.title: The Love & Lies of Rukhsana Ali
Jun.author: Sabina Khan
Jun.review:
4.5 rounded up.

Prior to The Love and Lies, I've never had a book I so fiercely related to. Rukhsana Ali was more than a character from a fictitious novel to me. She was an amalgamation of my friends over the years. Her struggle with feeling at odds with her family, workarounds to revealing clothing and leading a double life is a life a variety of my own friends lead. Women in South Asia are usually born into a role which is expected of them. However, with that being said, as we progress, it's easy to see how young South Asian women struggle to fit themselves into a single box feeling duplicitous as they behave a certain way at home and a certain way when away from the eyes of their community. It would be unfair to strip away one part of us and say we are one half of the double life we surround ourselves with. (To be fair, this might only ring true for some and that too is okay). Her friends found it hard to understand why she wouldn't just give up her family and walk away in face of everything they'd done to her where it became clear just how big the cultural divide was. The author gives us a glimpse into the Ali's daily life, coupled with days at the store, unannounced dinners with gossip-y aunties and full-fledged get togethers with the Bengali community of Seattle to build a sense of the circle Rukhsana grew up in and the attachment she's formed with her own identity as a Bengali Muslim over the course of several years.

What Rukhsana is subjected to as a queer person raised in a conservative household is the worst case scenario possible and somehow, the most realistic scenario possible. It pains me when I think about the horrors Rukhsana suffered through are not an exception but the reality of most LGBTQ+ people in Bangladesh. In the pages describing her agony, I felt panic, anger and desperation all at once, having to remind myself that this particular instance of hate crime inflicted by their own loved ones was only a work of fiction.

The writing fell flat when it came to Ariana and Rukhsana's relationship - a couple we were supposed to root for due to how much was at stake for them. Or maybe just Rukshana. In a book where everything goes to shit, you'd hope there would always be a silver lining. The silver lining here was Rukshana's support system comprised of Aamir, Irfan, Sara, Nani and Shaila. Sadly, Ariana and Rukshana's relationship, to me, was underdeveloped and just not that great. From the very beginning, we are aware of the main conflict threatening to burst through the seams of their relationship - Rukhsana was not ready to come out to her parents yet. She feared the consequences of this particular action, knowing fully well being gay in a Bengali family could very result you in being kicked out, disowned or locked inside the house forever. Rukhsana had secured a scholarship to Caltech, her dream school and was consequently worried that coming out before she graduated high school might mean her parents might no longer send her away to Caltech. In the face of this, she faced pressure from Ariana to come out, which should never be the case. If you're entering into a relationship with a queer person, you don't get to dictate when your partner comes out. Additionally, while we are told a lot about their love several times in the way of how they fight and make up immediately after, there's nothing to show for that love, making their romance a hard one to root for and Ariana, a character even harder to like.

When I talk about Rukhsana's support system, I truly can't appreciate the ones who saw her and loved her as she is in simple words. When I imagine Rukhsana's position, I can't begin to express the feeling of isolation which must have plagued her, knowing she's got all these people around her but none can truly understand what she goes through, however, her hope was maintained by her loved ones. Just as how blindly her parents were ignoring Rukhsana's pleas, she is backed by people who are ready to stand for her at every turn, even going as far as to help her escape. My favourite form of her happiness came in her familial bonds - her brother, who supported her throughout it all and was ready to risk his own relationship with his parents to stand by Rukhsana, her cousin, who helped Rukhsana navigate her way through Bangaldesh to form her own escape and gave steady advice and her Nani who was a well of wisdom and support for Rukhsana. Their relationship was so pure with the Nani guiding Rukshana at every step with words of strength and guidance, urging her to fight for a life of her own making and carve her own destiny. Her acceptance of Rukhsana shines a light on how bigotry and homophobia is not a generational issue but an issue with people refusing to bend their beliefs in the face of humanity.

spoilers in next para
While reading through reviews, I found many that lamented about Sohail's death being unrealistic. I want to cry and hold onto the hope that such a death could only be found in the pages of a novel and not out on the streets of Bangladesh. As someone who's been privy to the countless strikes activists take upon in Bangladesh, I know how it was like to hear that my friends were going to a protest and to hope that they'd come back alive, safe and sound. I wish this plot point was unrealistic but it's a reality that plagues the lives of those in the LGBT community of Bangladesh.

One of my biggest irks with the novel was her friends. To her credit, the author managed to display the privilege and entitlement that comes with being white which neither Rukhsana nor her parents can afford. From the very beginning, her friends downplayed Rukhsana's fears of her curfew or not being allowed to go the party at all, urging her to let it be because "surely it can't be that bad". This was frustrating on so many levels because later on, Rukhsana comments on how she's had to deal with initial qualms from her friend's family as "someone who won't blow them up" and Rukhsana, as a Muslim WOC, is just expected to understand and go along with this. She's expected to have intrinsic understanding of the fear people have of Muslims (internalised Islamophobia) and she's, more or less, supposed to be okay with her friend's parents thinking of her in this way. In a sharp contrast, we have her friends who fail to understand Rukhsana's culture and they don't try, to begin with. There's never a question of "Why do you have so many rules?" at any point in the novel. Somehow, her friends think that their own interpretation of the situation is correct and deem Rukhsana's to be incorrect or at the very best, dramatised. At no junction do they try to understand what she goes through or why she can't just come out to her parents. They have no idea why it may be life-threatening, as it is in several cases for South Asians, and dismiss it as "Oh they'll just ground you". At the end of it, overcome with guilt she shouldn't have, Rukshana is the one to initiate a conversation about her culture, feeling as though it were somehow her fault that her friends misunderstood her. Rukhsana's parents apologize to Ariana for their behaviour with her upon encountering the two of them kissing however, at no point does Ariana's mother come forward to apologize to Rukhsana for the harmful beliefs she held at the beginning.

Sabina Khan's novel, while very much about Rukshana, is also a love letter to Bengali culture and traditions. While I haven't been to Bangladesh in over two years now, the writing transported me right back to the busy roads of Dhaka feeling as though you'll never reach your destination in the throes of traffic. The dawaats, grand outfits and flashy malls filled me with joy because this is the part of my childhood that I resonate with.

The book end on a hopeful note with Rukhsana navigating her trauma and life while the community around her seems to be evolving to understand more about the sexual identity. The ending was crafted deliciously with light moments fleeting by while the family comes to terms with the past few months and opens up to each other.

Jun.author: Mary Gaitskill
Jun.review:
When you first click on this book, the top reviews have the following ratings : 3, 1 and 5 despite majority of those of us that read the book having the same takeaways but different interpretations of what the author conveyed. I fully went into the book, thinking I would hate it because for some reason, the reviews convinced me that this book sides with the abuser or tries to sympathise with the man, however, from what I understand of the text - very cleverly written by the author with points that either side of the #MeToo Movement could relate to - I think the broader point that stuck with me after the ending was : Why do women seem to comprehend the gravity of the situation more than men?

We follow two points of views - Margot and Quinn - who established an unlikely friendship about twenty years ago and this story explores the aftermath of accusations piling up against Quin ultimately losing his job while Margot continues to befriend him but is forced to question his seemingly innocent actions.

Quinn was highly unlikable, which is quite a feat to achieve in just about 80 pages, but somehow the author managed to paint him in the worst light ever. He thinks of himself as a practical jester, constantly flirting with women and texting them in times of crisis, however, time and time again, he forgets to respect boundaries, aggravating those around him only adding to their discomfiture. Did he have sex with them? Not quite - however, does it absolve him of passes made to women either younger than him or those working under him? No. The unequal power dynamic that settles in when someone who contributes to your professional career - only making you walk on eggshells when around them - or someone who can groom you due to the vast age difference between the two makes all the friendships he pursues dangerous. He has twisted views of the world and while he is painted to be a naive person, I don't think that's quite it. Time and time again, he downplays situations calling the paddle in his office a butter knife, taking women shopping and crossing boundaries with no consent just because he felt it was "sacred" and overall making the women around him uncomfortable. At one point, he refers to sexual abuse incurred by a character as something she did to have comfort the abuser.

Margot was the worst though. I understand that she feels Quinn has saved her life but to what extent do you owe your life to someone that you continue to forgive their missteps at each point? She reeks of preformative activism, writing a book that "empowers" women all the while taking delight in saying sexist things to those closest to her. When people bring up the unequal power dynamic, she refers to those women who couldn't say no as infantilized. At one point, she decides women are horses who must be led and want to be led but only in a way that dignifies them. However, she conveniently views each woman through the lenses of her own experiences, having been able to say No to Quinn when he tried to inappropriately touch her, she believes that each women who accuses him was wrong to not say No or be able to stand their ground. Unable to sympathise with the variety of situations of the victims, she continues to blame them - oh but you can't call the women witches, according to Margot, although calling them bitches is a-okay. At the end, she wonders whether Quinn should have lost his job and his honour as a human just because of this? Almost as if Quinn didn't breach the honour of his victims but okay. She thinks he should have been a laughing spectacle but not have his job ruined which was just an incredibly unsettling viewpoint to read about

For someone who has a bad track record with romances often ending up in dnfs, The Bromance Book Club was a pleasant surprise.

TBBC follows Gavin Scott on the brink of a divorce with his wife, serving as the wakeup call to the state their relationship is in. While desperately wanting to save his marriage, he reluctantly agrees to the help offered by his best friend, Del in the form of an undercover book club. The purpose of the book club, you ask? Men, in need of fixing their relationship and willing to go through growth, read romance novels to understand women's perspectives.

This book was an absolute delight to read and left a sappy smile on my face at all times. The main cast of characters are so endearing, in particular, the book club members who were the ones keeping the com angle of a rom-com alive her. I loved the way Gavin and Thea's relationship was laid out with conflict that felt real and stakes which seemed to affect the characters in drastic ways.

I loved the depth given to side characters, making them seem like real people which was done effectively without taking anything away from the main story.

All in all, men fighting for their family and going through self growth to put in the emotional growth required in a relationship with the help of their friends who let him have honest conversations, call him out in his bullshit and don't laugh at his shortcomings? why, yes, of course, that's a superior trope.

Jul.title: Local Woman Missing
Jul.author: Mary Kubica
Jul.review:
To its credit, Local Woman Missing has a very strong start. Delilah's POV is endearing and gritty, almost immediately making the reader root for her, holding their breath with her as she slinks away from her kidnappers and feel pure joy when it seems as if she's bought to justice. Part Two begins with the stormy night that took Meredith and Delilah away from Josh - we follow Meredith's neighbor, Kate who serves to bring the reader up to speed of the incidents that occur immediately after Meredith's disappearance. In addition, we have Meredith's POV, set a few months prior to her own disappearance, detailing her day to day life slowly inching the reader forward to the events that lead to the tragedy. Finally, we have Leo (Delilah's brother) as the side to explain all the events taking place in the "now", i.e., right after Delilah is found.

Despite the final "villain" being, more or less, predictable, this book was a page-turner with so many little twists going on at every corner and I couldn't seem to put it down, the thrill of finding the final puzzle piece keeping me at the edge of my seat. Additionally, the book delves into the lack of consent and general disregard of the mother's health during birth and post, where suspicions are chalked up to Meredith for having pills at her home from the time she had post-partum depression or Shelby's needs are neglected during birth with forceful pelvical exams despite her expressing discomfort. This book discusses these issues at length and let me question a practice which I, otherwise, wouldn't have.

With that being said, the book had too many red-herrings - a tactic which when employed perfectly can serve to misdirect the reader cleverly - however, in this case, none of the falsehoods had any sort of resolution leaving us with too many questions and no concrete answers (was the man following Bea and Meredith the OB/GYN or Jason? Who was the real father?)

Another problem was when details would be first mentioned serving the reader its intended purpose but would then be detailed at extensive length in another chapter with no actual payoff since the reader is already aware of how the situation ends. This particularly struck me when a midwife tells Kate and Bea about Shelby's birth, leading to a possible lawsuit against the OB/GYN, which is then detailed in a much later chapter but why should I read it when the fate of the baby is already known to me? Dueling timelines can be hard to pull off but particularly, aligning details in a way that is consequential and of importance to the average reader. The book also had a lot of fluff, which ties into the very first point, lots of points are included for the sake of including them but serve no purpose to the actual story other than leaving the reader to mull it over on their own. We get extensive details of Meredith's home-life and her practice as doula, despite not much of it affecting the main story. There is a plotline where Leo is bullied by someone at the sitter's home and I still don't understand how that contributed in any matter towards building a narrative. Consequently, there's a part where Kate and Bea decide to be amateur sleuths and investigate the OB/GYN themselves which has no payoff other than immediate shock value.

I still don't understand why we didn't get Delilah's POV since she was a character the readers were rooting for but apart from Part One, we only see Delilah through the eyes of her brother when it could have been a POV plunged in confusion and constant questions. This is not a problem as such but Mary Kubica can't write male POVs - Leo came off as super "pick me" nice guy constantly lamenting about how doesn't have a girlfriend, like do I care? In similar vein, the writing had lots of
telling the reader exactly what was going on, as opposed to show, which was so annoying because the author should at least trust their audience to be able to pick up on clues but instead, we get sentences like "Today Bea turns 30. This is her birthday party. They are here to celebrate" - this reads as if a bot was made to write prose.

Overall, this book was good for a quick read with lots of mindless twists and if you have a capacity for suspension of disbelief to the highest degree but look too closely at the plot and most of the narrative begins to fall apart to give something clearly implausible.

Jul.title: The Secret Keeper of Jaipur (The Jaipur Trilogy, #2)
Jul.author: Alka Joshi
Jul.review:
The Secret Keeper of Jaipur was one of my most anticipated sequels for 2021 after having read the first book in the series, The Henna Artist, early on in the year. Needless to say, Alka Joshi didn't disappoint as she brings forth a story brimming to the edge with hard-hitting questions of what makes a family and the revelations of internalized prejudices one may hold with class and social standing.

Set against the post-colonial India in early 1960s, we revisit Lakshmi and Malik, twelve years after the ending of THA, who now lead a quiet charmed life in the foothills of Himalayan Mountains at Shimla. Lakshmi has arranged for her protégée who now goes by Abbas Malik to intern with Manu Agrawal back in Jaipur, where work for the Royal Jewel Cinema is on the brink of completion, to learn the reins of business covering all fronts from construction to accounting. Malik finds himself in the throes of a mystery when the balcony for the theatre collapses during intermission, claiming two lives and leaving several wounded. The incident leaves a foul mark on the Palace's reputation who must find a man responsible for the construction as the scapegoat for pleasing public sentiments over the tragedy. However, Malik finds the situation to be amiss after discovering evidences of poor work done in the construction of the columns upholding the balcony in form of a decorative brick.

The stronger aspect of Alka Joshi's writing, for me, is the research that evidently goes into setting up the backdrops for her characters. I left the book with knowledge that no history book has ever taught me before - from the enlightening glimpse into the life of nomadic tribes to the callous ways gold was smuggled across the country for those willing to pay a hefty price after the Gold Act. Reading her books definitely serve to maintain a connection with a version of India that I have never been fortunate enough to witness or read about in the years that I've picked up reading. In addition to this, The Secret Keeper follows THA's footsteps in terms of rich descriptions filled with details of the surrounding, all the way down to the scent a place might have further allowing my own imagination to take flight and settle right at Mall Road of Shimla one minute and the chaotic beauty of Jaipur the next. The nostalgia and warmth I feel for the characters Alka has cultivated always takes me by surprise - so much so I am always rooting for them, smiling one minute at Lakshmi and her headstrongness and shaking my head when they act impulsive.


My only qualms for the books are definitely the characterization of Nimmi and the narrative decisions taken for The Secret Keeper. Coming to my first point, I couldn't find myself caring about Nimmi, whose POVs were sparse by the second half, or begin to understand why she was the way she was. What bothers me is that she's definitely supposed to be likeable, as is indicative by the prose, but the narrative doesn't her do any favors in terms of likeability every single time she lashed out at Lakshmi about Malik. This was to show us that their relationship was something that mattered a lot to Nimmi, having faced the loss of her husband and her tribe in her past and she was scared to lose Malik too - however, not enough narrative focus was given to their relationship which was wrapped up in a chapter and I didn't get why they even liked each other to actually care about Nimmi's fears. The justification we did get was that Malik liked strong women and that was that.

In ties to my first point, I think we had too many POVs jumbling up the narrative and not allowing there to be a distinctive voice to each of them. At one point, I was reading Malik's POV and thought I was reading Lakshmi's up until the halfway point of the chapter. While I understand Alka's attachment to Lakshmi, a character shaped after her own mother, I do not understand why this book was marketed as Malik's story when Lakshmi felt like the main character at several points with her own POVs dominating that of Malik's by the end. This is a story which could have worked very well with Malik's as the main POV, interspersed sparsely with Lakshmi's, to give the returning reader a taste of the headstrong lady we've come to love all the while acquainting ourselves with a much older and wiser Malik. Perhaps, the story should have introduced us to Malik's life in Shimla first as opposed to meeting him in Jaipur which could have made the reader more invested in his journey.

With that being said, I still think this book shines as one of the better written books I've read this year with a strong plot to hold it through the errs of narrative and characterization. I eagerly await the 3rd book in the series.

Sep.title: Not Here to Be Liked
Sep.author: Michelle Quach
Sep.review:
“Because everyone loves a girlboss until she tries to tell you what to do.”


According to the title and the publisher, Eliza is supposed to come off as unlikable. Reviewers say she starts off as unlikable and I couldn’t disagree further. I’ve been in the same position as Eliza - feeling that your identity is so closely linked to a club, a club you work tirelessly for that you think everyone around you is going to work just as hard for it but when they don't, you don’t get it. You don’t understand they may not love it as much as you do. Her peers were annoyed that she was so sure that she was going to be the editor-in-chief. The media we’ve been exposed to has always had us pitting for the female MC who’s an underdog - she doesn’t know how beautiful she is, she just isn’t aware of her worth and so every once in a while, when we do get a MC who’s sure of herself and who knows her qualifications make her worthy for a position, it makes everyone uncomfortable. Even us as readers with all our wokeness encompassed by instances of people getting cancelled on twitter will still stop and say, “oh but she is unlikeable”. I politely disagree because I simply don’t see why it makes us uncomfortable to see someone who knows what she wants.

Why are we not uncomfortable at the fact that someone decided to run for the position on the very last day as if it was so inconsequential to them but they can get it? Why are we not questioning ourselves as to why a woman must be well-dressed for a speech but a man can just show up and that’s all it takes? She’s told that “you try too hard which makes you unapproachable, you know what I mean?” at which point, my girl, the icon, says -

“No”, I say, “No, I do not know what you mean.”

The book hit so close to home that most of my annotations are angry mumblings of “fuck you” and “how would you feel if i just kicked you out of the milky way?” - a topic that feels all too familiar can do that to you. The initial misgivings of all those that said she cried wolf and that she should stop looking for attention made me so angry at the students in the moment but when I look back, it’s so reflective of the world we live in today. The newer generation is suitably woke, aided by countless resources and even more “#YouAreOver” trends on twitter, but in all of this, I do think microaggressions get a slip by. Veiled under the guise of dark humor, jokes and misplaced anger as instant as ramen, sexist microaggressions are evident, no matter where you look. We’ve internalised the broader picture of sexism in comparison of which, “one class president being female amongst a constant trend of males in the last decade” seems shining and a step in the right direction. Eliza’s relationship with her appearance was very well-developed. We start off the book with her sticking to a baggy sweatshirt and not putting much effort into her looks and her sister’s overbearing self about the same can get quite annoying but over time, you see how Eliza grows from her own experience of being the new feminist icon and finds herself more comfortable in her own body to be able to try out these things. The experience of finding things to be very black-and-white wherein assuming putting on makeup makes you any less of a feminist and submitting to the patriarchy was very prevalent in the past decade, bringing with itself the “not like other girls trend” - an attempt to create more division in women based on looks and how it correlates to how smart/successful you are, something Eliza suffered from at the start and it was great to see her character growth,


I loved the characters. There’s no question about that. My relationship with most of them was push-and-pull, the setting of Asian households feeling all too adjacent with my own upbringing (minus the internalised sexism, thank you mom). Beyond just Eliza, I really appreciated the depth bought to other characters like Len (my actual sweetheart bunny), Serena (my favorite trope over is mean girl assumed to be an airhead turns out to be an actual human with feelings and the main character bonds with them while feeling shitty about their assumptions) and Amanda (her conflicted feelings on participating in the rally at odds with the stereotypes of her own race and finding herself solitary in the way she felt was so well-done)

Len’s relationship with Eliza deserves its own paragraph. I don’t care, I make the rules of my review. They were adorable and I was positively gushing. Their first visit to the boba tea shop and him taking pictures of her was just cute - just give me wholesome couples is all I ask. This book has one of the tropes I adore which is, “MC reads books to talk about it/better understand their love interest” - it slaps every single time. Len was incredibly understanding and honestly, complemented Eliza so well. I was so happy with the route author chose to took and made Len a feminist icon instead of a sexist ex-jock who had to learn how to respect girls (gag)


recommended for anyone who's looking for a fresh YA romance with feminist themes and lots of drama

Aug.title: Project Hail Mary
Aug.author: Andy Weir
Aug.review:
This review alludes to situations which occur in the later half of the book and hence, may be spoiler-y

Andy Weir does it again. Reading Project Hail Mary was an incredibly transformative experience - when I picked it a few days back, I expected the genius I've come to expect when Weir is involved, of course but what I didn't expect was to be sobbing at the friendship formed by Grace and Rocky. For a book that was marketed as sci-fi, this book made me cry 3 times (when Grace says "Well, you're not alone anymore, buddy", when Grace goes back to save Rocky sacrificing his chance at life on Earth and when the book ended)

In a truer sense of the word, PHM is a thriller, an intense one at that - keeping the reader on the edge of their seats as conflicts come up with entirely believable baselines and you find yourself holding your breath, in how this may end. The stakes are so high that it's hard not to get emotionally invested in the characters - particularly when the French climatologist cried at what had to be done to offset the rate of extinction caused by Astrophage. The world I live in has not yet experienced a mass extinction event, leading my own life to be one of unprecedented comfort, so placing myself in a familiar setting only with the looming danger of extinction was hard but Weir does it brilliantly with the chaotic nature of how Stratt leads the operation, pulled back into reality with mentions of how the government have settled with the way Stratt run things but aren't happy about it or how corporations still fight over petty things seemingly small in the face of an apocalypse.

When DuBois and Shapiro die, Weir's red herring about their relationship plays brilliantly - leading the reader to believe that the explosion may have been caused because they were busy fraternizing - is that part of human error? Sure but it places the responsibility of that on two people in love. However, Weir's intended plotline shows human error on a grander scale where the unit accidentally hands a milligram of Astrophage as opposed to a nanogram. To the average human, differences in this scale is so miniscule that it would barely go unnoticed but it brings into perspective the weighty danger of playing with fire (literally) and the consequences of the same or how they trudge forward knowing the lives lost but with no time to grieve.

This book particularly hinges on friendship and how the universal experience of life and loneliness seems to be present in communities from microbes all the way to intelligent species. Rocky and Grace were my favorite duo ever written - they carry so much sadness, guilt and responsibility over their actions (or lack therof) and how it led them to Tau Ceti but the way they find each other and rely on each other for support and companionship literally broke my heart. Like, I am not joking, there exists a weird spider dude in the Weir-Universe who makes me sob and laugh and I love him so much. My face leaks when I think of him, it's a human thing, understand?

Grace's dry humor is so (in)appropriately placed. Yes, the world is dying and he may be the only one able to save it but he's still full of quips and retorts, often using humor as a coping mechanism in the situations he finds himself in and to avoid facing his own shortcomings. His character development is so amazing - he finds himself on a ship, suffering from retrograde amnesia with his memory coming back in bouts. He soon realizes what the ship's original mission was and sets about to complete it on his own, despite how originally he was too scared to go on the mission and give up his life. It's funny what the brain can convince you and how much you can push yourself once you convince yourself you can. The moment when the plot finally reveals his act of cowardice, it's a far cry from the hero we've come to see Grace as - the man who does EVAs in 1.5g or the man who learnt the Eridian language in a matter of few weeks or the man who gave his crew members the appropriate see-off even when it was hard - and that moment truly cements Grace as a human. An amazing scientist, a brilliant microbiologist with a flair for invention but ultimately, a human who can't fathom willingly dying. This is in stark contrast to the Grace we see in Ch-27 who rides off back to Tau Ceti to save Rocky, knowing fully well he's directly walking towards his death when he has a chance at survival. Their reunion is just so sweet. I love them so much. I can't deal.

This is all I have for now. Will I update when I think of more? Probably.

Oct.title: Iron Widow (Iron Widow, #1)
Oct.author: Xiran Jay Zhao
Oct.review:
this is one of my favorite books i've read this year and the one i'll probably credit in the years to come for reigniting my love for sff.

Iron widow is pitched as a reimagining of the lives of Wu Zeitan - China's only female emperor - against the backdrop of a world terrorized by strange aliens causing the government to develop giant transformer-like ships controlled by a male and female pilots by use of their qi. oh and the female pilot almost always dies in such endeavors and tragedy strikes Zeitan's family when her older sister dies in one such incident. Vowing to kill the man responsible for the death of her sister, Zeitan finds herself with more than what she bargained for, becoming entrenched in the mysteries of the oppressive system the government fights hard to keep secret.

Zeitan is an incredible protagonist and reading from her POV definitely made the story more enjoyable - she isn't the hero but the morally grey antihero, willing to sacrifice everything it takes to satisfy her own endgoals (as she should - let's go, girlboss!). She wants to destroy everything that she finds in this highly patriarchal world where the odds are stacked against her. Zeitan's anger was so prominent through the pages that I had my own teeth gritted, mentally screaming, "Kill them all"

I particularly enjoyed the emphasis on the continued pain in her feet - owing to the bounding ritual which took place when she was 5 - and am in awe of Xiran combined practices like foot binding in the futuristic world of Huaxia. Their depictions were incredibly moving and had me feeling phantom pain in my own feet.

The plot was incredibly engaging - I would be lying if it didn't take me a little getting into at the very start because the whole mechanics of the world were revealed, one layer at a time but as soon as she kills the male pilot, the plot picks up and never staggers even once. I finished the book in such a hurried frenzy, as if I couldn't stand to not know what happens next and if that doesn't tell you how good the book was, I don't know what will.

The poly M/F/M couple was not something I was privy to, prior picking up the novel but it was a great surprise and I love them all so much with all my heart - I only want more Shimin and Yizhi scenes, against the background of Yizhi's upbringing since I don't think we divulged enough into that. salted circus cashews, swear to god 5 stars
this is not a short story, at least i don't think so. to be honest, i am not too sure what clarifies as a story here but i think of this as the introduction to the entire book. this piece is most direct in what it's trying to convey - an allegory on relationships and how love is essentially putting blind faith into someone who might as well be a stranger, trusting them to treat you well and hoping this doesn't lead to heartbreak. most young adults have been through the cyclical facade of love - falling in and out, exhausted by yet another attempt at understanding another human and being disappointed when you find yourself crying over the same person who once gave you butterflies. it takes a fool to not turn a cynic in times like this, constantly cautious of what this new person could be in another day, week, month or year's time and you want to believe all their promises but somewhere deep down, you know these promises are the same one you make to others with no knowing if you can back them up in the future. god, i love this so much i could write a whole essay on the clever symbolism of the use of 'snake in a can' gag and marketing pitch to allude to vulnerability in relationships and the leap you essentially take, not knowing if you'll have a safe landing or if you'll fall in the cliff below.

Maybe you are right to be cautious. You have been lied to before, after all. Your heart is weathered and scarred, mishandled by many, eroded by time. You’re no dummy, and yet repeatedly, you stumble over the cracks of your cobblestone heart, you let your naked foolish hopes get the better of you.
And every time you discover the cruel fiction of the cashew can, you swear to yourself you’ll trust a little less next time, you’ll be a little less open, a little more hard. It’s not worth it, you say. It just isn’t worth it. You’re smarter than all that. From now on, you’re going to be smarter. Jun.title: Beyond the Gender Binary
Jun.author: Alok Vaid-Menon
Jun.review:
Our existence is made into a matter of opinion, as if our genders are debatable and not just who we are.
bumping it upto a 5!

i really enjoyed this book, i picked it up on a whim eager to support more queer authors writing nonfiction, in a bid to educate myself further and a general curiosity on existence beyond the gender binary and i couldn't have picked up a better book.

the book is incredibly accessible in its contents and written in such layman terms, making it ideal for anyone at any age with varying levels of information regarding the topic at hand. despite having substantial information about nonbinary identities, i left the book feeling like i had learned a lot and with an overall new perspective on not only those that identify as nonbinary but also on myself and the way i function as part of the world. alok vaid menon writes about their experiences existing outside the binary as someone who was "male passing" and bought into question a lot of biases, that we all tend to do almost subconsciously - microaggresions towards those that may not necessarily perform in accordance to the social norms dictating how they should act and essentially bringing in the conclusion that gender is a performance, the norms we've associated with each gender are more so a reflection of the societal culture at the time, as opposed to something just "intrinsic" to someone conforming to a specific gender.


i'll be linking a few of my favorite quotes here ☆

1. What I like about colors is that when you mix them together, they become greater than the sum of their parts, something different altogether. No one goes around asking, “But are you really more blue or more green?

2. Everyone thinks that since we “made a choice” to “look like that,” we are bringing it upon ourselves. The only reason people can fathom why we would look this way is because we want to draw attention to ourselves. They can’t even consider that maybe we look like this for ourselves, and not for other people. We are reduced to a spectacle. And when you are a spectacle, the harassment you experience becomes part of the show.

3. At a fundamental level, we are still having to argue for the very ability to exist.
The truth is, I still cannot go outside without being afraid for my safety. There are few spaces where I do not experience harassment for the way I look. Something as simple as running errands leads to strangers interrogating me about my body, trying to find some way to explain why I look like this. “Are you dressed up for a theater production?” “Oh, it must be Fashion Week again!”

4. It’s a surreal experience to have your personhood be reduced to a prop.
How are you supposed to be believed about the harm that you experience when people don’t even believe that you exist?

5.Gender non-conformity is seen as something immature, something we have to grow out of to become adults. Overnight, so many of the things that I loved not only became associated with femininity but with shame. Because I was a “boy,” I was no longer allowed to want to be a dancer or a fashion designer. Because I was a “boy,” I had to stop. Stop dancing. Stop being myself.

6.The thing about shame is that it eats at you until it fully consumes you. Then you cannot tell the difference between their shame and your own— between a body and an apology. It’s not just that you internalize the shame; rather, it becomes you. You no longer need the people at school telling you not to dress like that; you already do it to yourself. You no longer need your family telling you to be quiet; you already do it to yourself. You edit yourself, and at some point, it becomes so normal that you can’t even tell that you’re doing it. And the worst part is that you no longer have anyone else to blame.

7. Every aspect of myself was analyzed as either “masculine” or “feminine.” There was no in-between and nothing outside of these two options. “Why do you have so many friends who are girls?” “Why do you sit like that?” The idea here was that if you were a boy who displayed even a hint of femininity, then you were gay. And if you were gay, then you were wrong. And if you were wrong, that meant they had license to beat you up in the name of morality.

8. Truth be told, I don’t remember much of my childhood because I spent so much of it separated from my body. My body was where the shame lived, so I retreated into my mind. I was bullied everywhere, and it never stopped. It seemed so all consuming, like there was no escape. I became so terrified that my body would betray me—the hint of lavender in my voice, the sparkle in my gesture—so I sought comfort in my head, studying as hard as possible so I could one day get out of my town. I figured that if I was going to be effeminate, then I should at least be smart, to have something redeemable about me.

9. There’s magic in being seen by people who understand—it gives you permission to keep going. Self-expression sometimes requires other people. Becoming ourselves is a collective journey.

10. Society’s inability to place us in boxes makes them uncomfortable; the unfamiliar becomes a threat and not an opportunity. The unknown calls into question everything that we thought we knew about ourselves and the world.

11. The gender binary is set up for us to fail. For us all to fail.
The gender binary is more concerned with gender norms than it is with us. We are led to believe that there are only two genders, “man” and “woman,” and these genders are narrow, separate, and opposite. We are taught from a very young age that this is how things have always been and this is the only way to live. We are taught that masculinity belongs to men, femininity belongs to women, and that these are the only two options for self-expression.

12. At its heart, discrimination against gender non-conforming people happens because of a system that rewards conformity and not creativity. Rather than celebrating people who express themselves on their own terms, we repress them. This repression is something we first did to ourselves. We know how to do it so well to other people because we were the first testing grounds. We silenced our own differences, subdued our creativity, and toned down our own gender non-conformity in order to fit in. We thought fitting in would give us security—but is it security when someone else living their life differently unsettles us to our very core?

13. Depending on whether we call them a boy or a girl, we assign each a narrative—we tell some children that they are strong, and we tell others that they are weak. We tell some children that they can express themselves, and we tell others that they should not have feelings. We tell some children that their worth comes from doing harm, and we tell others that their worth comes from accepting it.

14.They say that gender non-conforming people, in particular, are caught up on some new fad: that we are inventing language, identities, pronouns, and genders. But language and grammar have always been developed to meet the needs of society. Consider words like selfie and welp, which have recently been added to the dictionary. This is actually the purpose of language— to give meaning to concepts as they evolve.

15. Being normative is about what gets elevated by society to a position of power. Normativity looks like a specific sneaker brand being upheld as the best. Normativity, then, is about value judgment and shouldn’t be used interchangeably with normal.It’s not that gender non-conforming people aren’t normal, it’s that we aren’t considered normative. Gender diversity is a natural attribute of human expression, not an illness that needs to be fixed. Gender non-conforming people face considerable distress not because we have a disorder, but because of stigma and discrimination. There is nothing wrong with us, what is wrong is a world that punishes us for not being

16. Pain does not have to be visible to be real, and violence does not have to be physical to be serious. Imagine everyone you encounter all day long telling you that you are not real and that there is something fundamentally wrong with you. Being constantly invalidated takes a toll: 40 percent of trans and gender non-conforming people have attempted suicide. Emotional and physical violence are not in competition with each other. It is possible to acknowledge one without invalidating the other.

17. Gender is not what people look like to other people; it is what we know ourselves to be. No one else should be able to tell you who you are; that’s for you to decide. Rather than considering the existence of multiple genders as a bad thing or even a good thing, why do we need moral judgment of it altogether? There are many ways that people can exist and describe themselves. Why is that a problem? We don’t consider remembering everyone’s individual name a burden; we just accept that as the way things work. Gender should be the same way

May.title: Perfect on Paper
May.author: Sophie Gonzales
May.review:
When asked about Perfect on Paper, I've pitched it as queer-centric Sex Education but with a lot more relationship advice carried out in complete secrecy. As someone going through a tough time, who latched onto attachment styles and intellcutalising everything to fit into boxes so things make more sense, this read came at a perfect time. Our main character identifies as bisexual, going through a tough time of her own - dealing with a crush on her best friend who doesn't seem to reciprocate - with another problem headed her way in the form of Brougham, a fellow student looking to fix his relationship with his ex-girlfriend in exchange for maintaining Darcy's secret of locker 89. The conversations revolving around queer teens, especially in the context of both sexuality and identity, were essential and were done with utmost respect and care, which I greatly enjoyed. The Queer Questioning Club felt like an actual integral part to Darcy's growth as a character, with a focus of its own, giving readers insight into problems queer teens may face at school and the author did a great job at making it a device important to both them and the story as opposed to having it feel like a throwaway, mentioned here and there, to move the plot forward.

Similarly, Darcy's responses to questions sent in by her peers were, not included at the start of most chapters, but referenced and used to further the plot in a way that felt meaningful. As someone, again, going through a tough time, in the context of the 'love/romance' department, this was actually super helpful. I am not too great at contexualising cues other people may give and it helps to see other characters, even fictional, deal with problems similiar to my own as a way to move forward, partly inspired by them. Additionally, yes, the one part where Darcy's sister calls her out for intellecualising everything to avoid feeling the emotions attached felt like a callout and I am thankful to the author because I needed to hear that, yep. Also the 36 questions to feel closer to someone? As someone who's not great at conversations or moving it along, I again thank the author for introducing me to this gem.


The banter between Brougham and Darcy was to die for, balanced equally with tender moments of vulnerability between the two. They got enough time together as they did apart, for it to still be Darcy's story as much as it was the story of her romance. I loved how the author integrated some very cute moments (cue: the rain scene followed by the movie) with moments where the characters opened up, let their guard down and just talked. As I grow older, I find myself wanting more and more of characters that just connect and this definitely served its purpose.

Also that one chapter on biphobia and feeling not 'queer enough' for dating someone of the opposite gender was just TOO real and i am really happy the author addressed biphobia, rampant both in and outside the community.

Sidenote because I am kinda tired of how much I've written but Brooke was just not it, idc.

Feb.title: Tokyo Ever After (Tokyo Ever After, #1)
Feb.author: Emiko Jean
Feb.review:
3.5/5

To the book's credit, when I first started reading it, I was sure this would be a 4.5/5 and if that didn't tell you how much I was enjoying it; I don't know what will. Tokyo Ever After will forever have my heart for making me squeal at 4am and giving me the Japanese Princess Diaries I wanted. Yes, it's cliche and yes, it still executes them well. I really enjoyed the romance - there's just something about forbidden we-can't-be-together romances that hit different. Izumi's growth was so pleasant to read about and I am excited to follow the second book to see more conversations on the inherent patriarchy embedded in the imperial system dealings - also, highkey, I just want a book about Hanako x Makoto hashing over their Harvard romance to their reconciliation. The scenes in Kyoto were definitely my favorite - written with so much love and reverence, I could feel the peace emanating through the pages.

Moving onto things I didn't like which, more or less, ruined things for me. The pacing was off. The first half of the book moves at a slow pace, setting the characters and background well. However, the second half presses down on the accelerator hard with things that one would think would take a bit more resolving getting thrown out of the window in a chapter (Think Izumi's kiss which, when being a onetime event, just quickly followed into a succession of more? I didn't feel connected to it because of how many times the stakes were reiterated over the course of the book). Similarly, for the last plot twist, I feel like the author just created things from thin air, regressing the development of an entire character to fit a narrative when no such inkling was given before. Had she hinted at it early on in the book, as sure-fire signs that would strike the readers as odd but one that would be dismissed by Izumi, the reveal would have been more satisfying instead of feeling like it was created at the last minute to resolve said conflict.

Aug.title: The Measure
Aug.author: Nikki Erlick
Aug.review:
The premise sounded like something I could expect Tiktok POVs to have but to my pleasant surprise, Nikki Erlick used this premise to offer an empathetic look at how as situation like this upends the world on a global scale and more importantly, on an individual.

In the days since I've read this book, I have become an absolute menace to everyone positing 'what-if' questions about their strings and the people who'd live to face the consequences. The Measure provides a very humane look on people, love and relationships - it doesn't just hinge on 'short-stringers' but the people around them. The characters struggle to accept that their/their loved-ones' lives may end so soon - the dual approach that many people take is also interesting; people either leave their jobs, move away and travel to live their remaining years with no regret or they struggle to cope with the knowledge of a short life, their regrets mount and they use their short time to exact revenge on others or cause accidents on a wide scale. That's on an individual level but as for global, the story repeats as it has in the history of the world - as much as humans are united against the face of adversary, our textbooks prove that time and time again, humans find comfort in discrimination - in othering others to protect themselves - this reassures us that we are safe & inadvertently, better. While the commentary was a little on the nose, this book offered a fresh look at the discrimination that plagues our 'now', short-stringers used to forward political interests, fear-mongering of an experience the long-stringers don't understand, reduced opportunities (jobs, bank loans, promotions etc) - all speak of a world we are familiar with today. The face of discrimination has changed, yes, but the discrimination remains there nonetheless.

While essentially general fiction guised as speculative sci-fi, it poised a lot of good questions -
Would I open my box? If I knew I had little time left, would I continue living the way I was? Would I date a short-stringer? Marry them? Have children with them? Would I fake my results to ensure I am not discriminated against?

I would love to say I have all the answers but I don't.

Mar.review:
until you've experienced the nihilist deadland that is modern corporate life punctuated by passive aggressive smiley faces & no concept of work life boundaries, this book might not be for you. is it odd? very much so - your only frame of reference for the narrator and the characters is just their slack messages, something that isn't necessarily revealing of true personalities and you only know what they tell you. somewhere between a satire and a really smart sci-fi, this book will understandably make you laugh and if it doesn't, i am probably the oddity for laughing my heart out at 4am and depuffing my eyes at 6am to prepare myself for work the following day. despite all of this, looking at my notes and highlights in front of me, i can also tell you this was a really smart book with observations that you wouldn't expect out of a book like this - case in point :

By that logic, a relationship is just a cult with two people. Well, okay, two or more people. A shared language, shared rituals, devotion to ideals like “fidelity” or “love” or “getting really into Renaissance Faires together.”
and
you’re a few finger-flicks away from an unending stream of human rawness exported to posts and pixels but even if you’re not looking or if you can’t look (because staring at the sun for more than a few moments is bad for you) it’s still there, everyone’s still posting, still there to be beheld
and
but if the only part of you that you can consciously experience is your consciousness’s experience and if all of that focus is 100% turned on to the dumbest fucking bullshit you’ve ever read in your life and that’s what you’re thinking about and since you’re all thoughts all the time that’s all that you are.
and
kind of like an extreme version of being on twitter or something
looking into thousands of different people’s lives at once
we’re not made to absorb this much human information at once, man. all the pathos and bathos and other thos-es
I’d say it’s exhausting except I can’t feel tired and anyway it’s beyond that
it’s overwhelming for a species that was basically content with an oral tradition of a handful of long-ass stories about the same six shitty gods for millennia

this book manages to capture the increasing need of staying connected in times likes ours where we're consuming more content each day than we probably did 15 years ago in a year and the sort of dread that comes with it- you have to stay connected but in doing so, what are you really gaining? you might log off but what happens if you miss the latest drama and how did you convince yourself you should care about the newest celebrity surgery pandemic?

it's also the perfect horror for the modern corporate employee (me) where the only people you can conceivably speak to is your employees because you're spending all your time at work and you've no other real connections beyond it so when your consciousness somehow does get uploaded onto slack, you're left badgering your coworkers to believe you because they're the only people you speak to but more importantly no one seems to find it odd that you're sending mails at 4am because you're being more productive than ever, you're a go-getter! a real team player a dependable employee so suddenly you're no longer being fired, your wfh is approved despite being a point of contention in the past and you realize you're just a cog in the machine.

also just point in case about how easy it is to become attached to people you've never met - i genuinely felt like i knew these people despite yknow not even knowing their true characters but just their work persona!
