Jan.title: The Villa
Jan.author: Rachel Hawkins
Jan.review:
How often are we bright stars in someone else’s sky, but they couldn’t find us with a fucking telescope, huh?

The Villa is full to the brim with an idyllic setting at a villa I'd sure love to visit, two best friends reunited but with conflicting feelings and a murder that takes place in the 70s at the peak of rock n roll. A revealing story about womanhood, how easy it is to get lost in someone else, choosing yourself and paving your own path. Oh, and murder, of course. Overflowing with reveals that especially picked up at the very end, The Villa is not what it seems at first glance - you have your fleetwood mac-esque typical 70s rockstars and their hanger ons partying in a summer when things go very very wrong. The women these rockstars string along to hang onto their every word pave their own way finding themselves at the front of a career post murder and become famous in their right but is there something darker lingering beneath the clear cut murder sentence? The villa they stayed in has been inhabited several times since then but most notably finds itself at the brink of another murder half a century later when childhood best friends make their way to the villa for six weeks. Did I tell you they are writers desperately trying to get their next book out? That should make for a fun read and it did!

Rachel Hawkins nails the story capturing the vibes of the 70s so beautifully and alternatively making each timeline interesting slowly building the suspense. My only critique, akin to what I felt at The Wife Upstairs, would be that the pace is always so off - the books start off so slow at a snail's pace that I feel like I am drudging along only to pick up at the very end but good thing she does unique plots justice

Jan.title: All the Dangerous Things
Jan.author: Stacy Willingham
Jan.review:
5 stars because not only did I finish it in one sitting but I am sitting wide awake at 4:30am marveling at this thriller.


All The Dangerous Things follows all the typical makings of a thriller - an unreliable narrator, a stranger looking to solve the case, a mystery in her past and a fractured family in the present but Stacy Willingham does something truly marvelous with all these cliché elements - she creates a story so distinctly her own. It could be my own disillusionment speaking at the feeling of finally ripping through a book in one sitting but to be able to constantly keep the reader interested even when the twists are obvious is a feat all on its own. The pacing and structure of this book is incredible - all the twists come at the right spots, the reveals are clever and the foreshadowing brilliant. The book is fast, happening over the span of a few days, keeping me on my toes constantly and it gets right the one thing a lot of thrillers don't: flashbacks. The flashbacks in this book were sprinkled in throughout the narrative revealing the story little by little which was perfect.

The then part was giving me haunting of bly manor and that's all the push i can give you to read the book! The does such an unexpected reveal on the biggest true crime cliché (100 points if you get it) - I had the killer pegged 1 hour in but the road to get there was so good, it was worth it.

Jan.title: A Magic Steeped in Poison (The Book of Tea, #1)
Jan.author: Judy I. Lin
Jan.review:
“There is a difference between living the suffering and reading about it.”

A Magic Steeped in Poison is exactly what you would need when you crave comforting tea and a high-stakes show in the background. Interlaced with the competition in a bid to be the court's resident shennong-shi, the overarching mystery of the traitor within the court and the political intrigue in the book, the stakes are incredibly high in this book making for a read that eventually turns unputdownable. What really sold this book for me is the seamless weaving of mythology and use of ancient chinese practices forming the foundation of the magic system in the book. It's very important for the magic systems in books to be no longer reductive and explore + push boundaries as far as they can - safe to say, a magic steeped in poison has a beautiful, vivid and unique take on magic. Tea as a way to connect, soothe and heal is a love language so special to the global south where the very first thing we do when a weary loved-one comes back or a guest is at our house is offer them tea. It's more than just a drink, it's a way to form connections with the other persons - conversations held over warm tea have the power to invigorate you. A warm cup when drank alone in a bout of homesickness is enough to return you to the feeling of home for a moment and offer you peace. I love that the book really respected not only the art of making tea, a magic all on its own balanced on the ingredients you choose, but also the medium tea provides you when consumed with someone else to be able to link you with them.

The political intrigue was incredibly well done especially with Ning at the forefront of it all, dealing with two-faced individuals at every turn and not knowing who to trust beyond the barest of few who fell under the working class. The critique of capitalism and the concept of the 'rich frolicking by while the working class toils for them with no reprieve from taxes' was integrated very well and you can feel the sort of burden the blue-collared individuals live in this book. Ning was an a pleasure to read about; not only did she have the conviction to make the reader root her but she constantly made decisions that seemed to have an uniform line of thought. She was very strong in the face of danger but more importantly she was someone who was very skilled in her art and that made her just all the more interesting. Her loyalties were unwavering and I loved the way she defaulted to spending time in the kitchen feeling more at home there where everything was the way it seemed. Her internal conflict is very well fleshed out and I cannot wait to read about how she overcomes it in the coming book, forgiving herself for her past mistakes and moving forward with the knowledge she has now that she didn't then. Her relationship with Kang is still new - I am equal parts delighted and frustrated that Kang didn't have his own narrative focus beyond his time with Ning where we learn about his past because I like him and I want to read about him! But I get the choice the author made in choosing to keep us in the dark like Ning is, making their relationship believe because if I am enamored, I understand why she is!

ALSO NEED TO MENTION THE SAPPHIC PRINCESS X HANDMAIDEN? I need more.


My main critiques are mainly the pacing which seemed to pick up at the end with a lot condensed into very little when that spread of plot over pages could have been more even. The descriptions were also very flowery and while exorbitant in nature, I couldn't imagine a lot of the places detailed, after which I began to skip them because the prose was not adding up with the vibe established like I cannot bring myself to care about the way the garden looks when someone is about to die.

Jan.title: The Six Deaths of the Saint (Into Shadow, #3)
Jan.author: Alix E. Harrow
Jan.review:
i know him, and in knowing him i love him, and in loving him i cannot do as he wishes

It is simply unfair that Alix has the power to say so much in so little because little did I know while going into a seemingly short story that it would play with my emotions so much. The Six Deaths of the Saint is beautifully tender in its portrayal of love and belonging - the writing is incredibly lyrical and only adds to the narrative prowess of the story. I did not expect that the story would as complex as it was with several twists taking me completely by surprise and the main character was stripped layer by layer revealing a little bit more about herself each time around.

Alix speaks of the desire to belong, to be somebody who's needed when they've spent their lives discarded, the price of power and blind devotion and how that can drive you to change your perception in your fierce need to be desired. A story about walls of delusion we build to lull us into a sense of safety and the blind eye we turn to maintain the reality we never had chasing the conditional love - how that often turns into a well of its own leaving us there entrapped in a place of our making and how connection with care for us and love us for who we are has the power to change all of that. And for all of this to be written by an author who so obviously cares about her characters and the way she tells her story makes for an incredibly reading experience.

Okay, I need to reread all my favorite scenes all over again

Jan.title: House of Hunger
Jan.author: Alexis Henderson
Jan.review:
Read as part of BooksandLala Literally Dead Book Club

House of Hunger was a book that really found its footing story-wise around 20% in which is the point I would say, I was completely invested in it and started having a lot of fun. Having read Year of the Witching and now House of Hunger, I can safely say Alexis Henderson will become a go-to for gothic historical fiction because I believe she is able to describe the surroundings so vividly and the central conflicts of her books are always interesting. House of Hunger is a gothic tale set in 1800s where rich nobles of the North often take up bloodmaids, usually from the poorer regions surrounding them including the South, where we follow a young girl, Marion, looking to escape her life of servitude and financial instability with the prospect of being a bloodmaid for Countess Lisavet for the House of Hunger where she makes new companions in the residing bloodmaids. Her fairytale life is ruined by the seemingly shady practices she notices that goes on at the House.

Marion was a very interesting character to me - not all her choices were smart but they made sense in the context of her situation where she lets herself be so enamored by Lisavet and turns a blind eye to the obvious for a while because you can tell, she wants to believe so badly that she can have this seemingly perfect life. I loved the clues Alexis has peppered in throughout the book about the main "mystery" and finding the threads to correlate them was so much fun as a reader.

real talk the death of the house mother was probably more satisfying than lisavet like the house mother had no reason to be acting the way she was and she got what was coming to her

Where House of Hunger faltered is the pacing. The first 10-15% (although it felt much longer) focused entirely on Marion's life before and her journey to becoming a bloodmaid in extensive details which was honestly quite slow and my reading experience would have been better if this was wrapped in 2/3 chapters as opposed to dedicating a good screen time of the book to this part which, ultimately, does nothing outlining her character beyond her resilience and desperation in escaping her circumstances. The part focused on Marion's introduction to the House, the bloodmaids and the Countess was very well-done but we again encountered issues when it came to the conflict and the calm before the storm. Marion's period of bliss with Lisavet was covered in one chapter and while you're ultimately not meant to root for this borderline Stockholm Syndrome relationship, I would have liked to see some degree of chemistry between the two - there was no clear understanding of why Marion was attracted to Lisavet beyond her beauty and the inherent gratitude Marion feels towards Lisavet for being pivotal in her escaping the North. My main problem is the conflict/climax which is a part of the blurb and makes up for very little of the book - it is made to look like such a big part of the plot with the whole 'bloodmaids start disappearing' when that is clearly to mislead the reader and not enough attention was paid to fleshing out the cracks in Marion's fairytale - it just feels like she stumbled into the mystery. I also wished Alexis would commit to the mystery - the 'Wretch' written everywhere was overlooked, the mushroom mentioned in Lisavet's back story felt like it had a potential to tie back in a satisfying full circle way

Overall, I vastly prefer House of Hunger to Year of the Witching - the themes of power dynamics, exploitation of the poor, hunger, girlhood, what it means to choose when the stakes are off balance and the house as entity which quite literally feeds on you were very enjoyable against a compelling backdrop.

Jan.title: Everyone Dies Famous in a Small Town
Jan.author: Bonnie-Sue Hitchcock
Jan.review:
this book is unassuming in its own brilliance in a way that it wouldn't be a complete understatement to say how much the blurb undersells the book - if i am being completely honest, i picked up the book because of the beautiful cover but the very first story was enough to hook me in. set in different parts of the US from Alaska to Pigeon Creek to Granville, each story holds center to itself a small town and characters linked to every other story in one way or another, in a way that's so beautiful and lyrical while still being completely accessible to anyone new to bonnie-sue's writing.

with pivotal themes centered around grief, memories, secrets and the mundanities of life, this book made for a very quiet heartwarming read, often reminding me of fredrick backman's style of observing characters and capturing their emotions. i loved how poppy was central to all of this despite her secondary role in the first story, something which i think is reflective of the whole book. stories of angry teenagers finding the empathy within in difficult situations and accepting a new family, of first loves and the way they're lost bringing everything else into perspective, of very popular girls with shaky histories and an ambition that outdoes the quiet seaside they come by and how it manifests in ugly ways, young queer love and accepting yourself when placed in a town that views you as wholly different, of catholic priests who get away with abuse for far too long and young children unable to express what happened with parents who don't listen close enough because the truth isn't clean-cut and young girls who find the strength within themselves to put an end to it all leaving fires in their wake, of a town quite like beartown and an obsession with a sport where you're never given a choice of if to play or not but you're always an outsider if you don't and questioning whether being good at something is the same as liking it, of friendships and a camp with children like no other, the eventual downfall of a man more trusted than entire departments, the wildfire that creeps into our lives blowing everything wide open and unexpected token of kindness by strangers often become becaons of hope.


god, i loved this book. my favorites were probably the right kind of people and there's gas in the tank, louise!

Jan.title: And Every Morning the Way Home Gets Longer and Longer
Jan.author: Fredrik Backman
Jan.review:
i find it very difficult to articulate the experience of reading a backman book - sometimes i wonder whether the very fact that i have read such life changing books by him has forever biased me towards him and anything he writes or is he genuinely so good of an author that i will forever like everything he has to say in the way he says it? truth be told, the answer probably falls somewhere in between these two. i loved this novella very much with all my heart and yes, at points, i did ask myself if the concept is too simplistic for me to be in tears over it but the fact is backman captures life in a way that feels so authentic with so much heart, it's difficult not to like it.

interspersed with memories of his wife, his son and his grandson, this book paints a portrait of a very smart man with a few regrets up his sleeve and a lifetime of beautiful experiences, who is facing imminent death and slowly losing the one thing he holds precious : his memory. within 100 pages, we are introduced to 'Grandpa' and Noah, placed within a hospital room, his brain, his house and his boat, building a beautiful story of grief, loss, love and a life well-lived. you can feel the confusion and sadness grandpa feels at the gradual loss of his memories, the love built on a foundation of pure understanding and like-mindedness between grandpa and noah, a lifetime of regrets and trying to bridge it between grandpa and ted and most poignantly, the love shared between two individuals who've lived hundreds of experiences together for grandpa and his wife.

Sep.title: I Feed Her to the Beast and the Beast Is Me (I Feed Her to the Beast, #1)
Sep.author: Jamison Shea
Sep.review:
Books with a villain/anti-hero MC are typically a hit-or-miss for me. When done well, it can be so satisfying but when done poorly, it will remind of this book. The concept was such a win - ever since watching Black Swan, every ballet book just has instant intrigue from me.

What did not work for me unfortunately was the prose - I like beautiful writing, don't get me wrong but when the beautiful writing is used as a prop to encapsulate the lack of concept, I don't enjoy it. We did have a concept of Acheron and Lethe but the background context to it just wasn't good enough - at no single point did I feel like I had an understanding of what the author intended because we started with this foreboding sense of the monster slowly taking over Laure and how she was almost afraid of what she would become and by the end of it, the monster is almost shown to be a sympathetic character and I feel like I missed the progression which would explain such a contrast in viewpoints.

The love plotline was so stilted and weird and felt very out of place like it was immensely jarring to finish a chapter with gore and violence and suddenly, they're kissing? Like what? The murder plotline is something that is started to drive the plot forward but almost immediately abandoned with no real findings from Laure but just hypotheticals strewn in here and there and the answer to this plotline is too conveniently just thrown in her lap as opposed to be something she looks for.

Just no.

Sep.title: Goddess of the River
Sep.author: Vaishnavi Patel
Sep.review:
I once thought I knew the Mahabharat. In many ways, this book proved me wrong.

The book follows a river-like flow wherein initially it started off slow and confusing but like the story it tells, it crescendos into a high and creates an engaging narrative with themes many readers would be forced to think about.

This book forced me to think about my own position on the actions these characters took - Vaishnavi says it best when she says no one who was a part of Mahabharat was without faults and did misdeeds, it matters ultimately what the weight of those choices are. If you didn’t do what you had to do in those circumstances, what would have happened? Would that path be better than the one you are forced to take?

Every character was so profoundly complex - often times, I boil down this great epic that every Indian kid knows to the ‘good’ side Pandavs and the ‘bad’ side Kauravs but this book (and ultimately the Mahabharat) has provided so much background to these characters- are the good ones really good when they are presented with choices of gamble, misbehaviour, forgoing the rules of combat and acting as if they are beyond reproach? are the bad ones really so bad when you see instances of their humanity, empathy, bonds they’ve created, friendship and loyalty? ultimately you choose to abide by your belief of righteousness and you will always have people who don’t agree with you and what you do in these moments define you. The text was so deeply engaging in terms of dharma and adharma, conversations several characters have showed the multiple perspectives.

The exploration of bounding yourself to a belief, unwilling to change in the face of injustice to stand by your belief and how ultimately selfless intentions don’t always result in selfless actions was so beautiful and honestly, i know a retelling has done a good job when it makes me want to reread the original, Vaishnavi’s beautiful writing is always a plus (there are so many quotes i loved)

Mar.title: The Girls I've Been
Mar.author: Tess Sharpe
Mar.review:
3.5

The Girls I’ve Been takes up a concept I’ve never read before and turns into truly something worth listening 9h of audiobook of. It takes concepts of a bank heist and turns into something truly phenomenal because who could’ve guessed that the opportune day the robbers choose to rob the bank, there’s a con artist and an arsonist in the mix?

One of my gripes with media has always been showcasing fairly traumatic situations and characters bouncing back from it like it was nothing, however, here we toggle between the present and the past, a lot of which is traumatic and due justice is given to the characters in acknowledging the shitty situations they found themselves in and the effect it had on them and their lives. The plot is well-structured with little to no lulls/filler content in between which makes for an exciting read giving the story layers of complexity.

Where the book misses the mark, for me personally, is marking it as ‘Young Adult’ and having the characters be teenagers when the voice/tone of the story/characters felt very adult and it would’ve been more cohesive for them to be 21-23. The only reason I feel it was YA is purely for marketing reasons since YA is a lot more sellable than Adult. Similarly, shelving it as ‘Thriller’ does the book no favors because the stakes never felt high, it always felt like it was inching to a resolution that was a happy ending for the main cast and at no point, was I worried about the heist ending poorly for the trio.

I feel like this is the work that I’ve been so confident is the book that deserves three star like this is a three star book. I loved the set up and the plot behind this book, however, would that being said the problem with this book is that it was always building up to something, but I feel like it never quite reached that. in part, the description does the book dirty because the description mentions the great grandson learning about Meher but we never quite see that happen in the book.

The dual POV does not do the story justice because there are so disconnected that it feels like you’re reading two completely different narratives with no parallels between them - in part. it happened because the author wanted to touch on a lot of different themes, but they were not really connected such as the patriarchy, oppression of women, the partition and racism faced by Indians abroad.

In addition to that, the great grandson’s narrative was just not interesting like it had nothing going for it except for a lot of exposition that ultimately led to no payoff - I like this book because it was a quick read and ma’s POV was incredibly interesting, specially in the glances where we get to see her home life and her married life, and getting used to a whole new way after living, a life of freedom. What me about the story however, is that we get no payoff again for what may end of being and what her story sums up to.

my only gripe with this is that the setup which lasted about 30% of the way took too long and was incredibly descriptive making it incredibly boring but once the deaths started happening, it got way way more enjoyable

Jan.title: On a Sunbeam
Jan.author: Tillie Walden
Jan.review: my favorite thing about this book was just how quiet this was, and I don’t think it’s entirely easy to explain what I mean by quiet, like yes, it was low stakes, but that is not what I mean. What I do mean is that I just enjoyed the found family for our main character Mia - I enjoyed how everyone had very fleshed out characters and ultimately i just like how mundane and unique this concept was. You don’t often see a space opera with the world so complex but at the same time, the focus is on the characters. We learn about the world in bits and pieces but the characters never lose focus in any of this. You don’t get a big adventure where all of them are of fighting a big big war, but you do get see them doing day-to-day tasks. My favorite thing was just the interactions that the characters had it felt so organic and genuine but most importantly, it just felt like these people were friends because they just liked each other and each other’s companies and I just enjoyed that. Obviously, this review would be incomplete without me, mentioning the art which was simply gorgeous. There were so many panels that were actually breathtaking that I had to stop for a minute and just soak it in. This was one of my favorite experiences ever in terms of reading a graphic novel, and to think I was about to DNF it.

Nov.title: Murder by Memory (Dorothy Gentleman, #1)
Nov.author: Olivia Waite
Nov.review:
3.5

There is a dangerous line you walk with novellas. A brilliant novella never feels limited by its length. It carries you effortlessly through its story, making you laugh and cry with its characters, and builds a world so vivid it’s hard to believe it fits within just 200 pages. It is just as easy to mess up and do the exact opposite of that where you leave the reader wanting for more but for all the wrong reasons.

All of this is a roundabout way of saying this book fell somewhere in the middle for me.

The world was brilliantly built; the concept of uploaded memories and your memory extending your lifespan was so unique and the spaceship hosting an entire mini-city fully functional felt very authentic SF. Sadly, for me, what did not work as well was the mystery - it was extremely underwhelming. We spent a lot of time just learning the world since our character had been asleep for two years and was getting introduced to a lot of the new systems in place which took away from the mystery. It feels like we walk into the resolution a bit too conveniently.

I will continue reading the series and give it another go since I am still interested in the world but I hope the author builds out Dorothy a bit more - I'd like to learn more about her personality that does not contain like knitting and tea but more substantial stuff (like her trying out summer storm and the evocative feeling it brings with it!)

Nov.title: Not Quite Dead Yet
Nov.author: Holly  Jackson
Nov.review:
This really worked for me - i've had my eyes on this for the longest time and the only thing stopping me was how boring the first chapter was. I started this book 2-3 times and would drop it every single time because October 31st did not work for me, however, I pushed through solely because of how great the reviews were on my feed.

Thank god I did, because I had such a good time with it. Holly Jackson writes unique mysteries every single time which is difficult to do in an severely oversatured genre run over with tropes and she delivers every single time. This particular one had so many different little twists, some of which I guessed, others which had to be spelled out for me to get it - the book was unputdownable and the reading experience was very enjoyable.

The only redeeming characters in this book was Billy and the dog who really were caught in the crosshairs but we had an elaborate list of side characters, all of whom were given distinct personalities and felt like people as opposed to carciatures which is difficult to do in a book with so many arching plot points.

One other thing I loved about the book was Jet's realisation about what life means for her & how life can't be resolved by an overarching goal that always feels out of reach but chasing happiness in the little moments of your life - I feel like that is a message that will always be timeless across all stages of life.

My only issue was that this book did not feel like an adult thriller? If the same book was published with nothing modified except Jet's age to 17, the book would still read exactly the same. I hadn't even realised this was Holly's foray into adult thriller and while I wept into the inside of my pillow at the end, nothing about this was very *adult* thriller.

Oct.author: Patrick  O'Dowd
Oct.review:
3.5 (rounded off to 3 because it is the year 2025 and Goodreads still does NOT have half star ratings)

This book is incredibly relevant in the current socio-political climate. One of the best done parts of this book explores Tess & Richard Welch; not only is the rallies and talks organised by Richard in the book directly inspired from the ongoing events but it also gives us this insight into not only what attracts attention and unwavering loyalty to these public figures but also the charisma & tactics employed by them to skirt the line of what is legal and illegal, inciting violence by words and overall drawing some important spotlight to the fact that words are just as bad as being the one to light the building on fire if they are unchecked.

I also enjoyed seeing Tess as this unwilling victim of becoming a spokesperson for the other side, having her own words controlled and set up as this beacon of worship, paralleling Richard Welch.

Ultimately what annoyed me is some of these plot points felt edgy for the shock factor (the parties) and a lot of the revelations came too late in the book - the Jack thread was promptly abandoned and picked right back up out of nowhere and I feel this book could have been an even more profound book if we had 1-2 threads we were following throughout vs trying to do a commentary on multiple things at once.

I would have also enjoyed a bit more characterisation with respect to our main character who mainly just acts as the eyes for us to view the events but we never learn enough for her to feel for her and what happens to her.

Would definitely recommend this book for anyone looking to understand the current political climate in USA.

Sep.title: Severance
Sep.author: Ling  Ma
Sep.review:
While I enjoyed the story and I enjoyed the conversation around capitalism and how it extracts work from you until it literally sucks you dry. This is driven further by how you’re doing the same thing over and over even when you are literally fevered. It was also a love letter to New York, or at least a letter to New York, how it has been taken away from the people who made it to serve those who work in shiny glass buildings and skyscrapers. There are ruminations about the experience of being an immigrant and how Candace is the way she is because her parents asked her to be useful and that is a uniquely immigrant experience/need alongside the whole millennial thing

While I get all of that, I feel like the same were a little on the nose which is fine as long as there was something going on on the plot. Up until the end, we were following the plot very well (albeit being so dull) until we had an abrupt ending, which feels very weird for the reader because we’ve been following this character we’ve been watching her move through different landscapes and the ending doesn't provide closure of any sort. Everything doesn't need to be told, yes but a plot needs to move forward - you cannot choose a midpoint on it and deign it to be the ending.

This book felt like it desperately wanted to provide commentary trojan horse-d as a story - a lot of it is explained away because our main character goes through life thoroughly emotionally detached from her own body & surroundings. But reducing your side characters to caricatures with no real defining features, explaining away plot holes and introducing many moving parts cannot be completely explained just with her own characterisation. I feel this book could've benefited from honing in on 2/3 themes as opposed to including everything in a fairly short book that dragged the worldbuilding and character development down.

Aug.author: George Orwell
Aug.review:
George Orwell is someone I’ve heard so many good things about but was always afraid to pick up something written by him due to the assumption that a classic is going to be difficult to read. When my book club picked this as the book of the month, I asked for six weeks to read it because I thought I was gonna log through it so imagine my surprise when I realised how readable this book is. due to the subject matter and what the book talks about, I really thought that it would be inaccessible when, in fact, I feel like the author made it accessible because of the demographic that most needs this.

1984 “imagines” a world where people are under constant surveillance and monitoring via the use of TV and print media is basically fiction that the government completely controls. The word is divided into three subcontinent who are constantly fighting, and the people in these three subcontinents live in the constant fear of war. The understanding is is that if everything can be monitored, there can be no internal attacks and you assume the government wants what’s best for you, so you give them privacy over your own thoughts until you are so propaganda-fed that you don’t know what your own thoughts are anymore.

[SPOILERS AHEAD - ANALYSIS OF TEXT FOR BOOK CLUB DISCUSSION]

Our main character works in one such faction of the government intended to rewrite history to ensure that all of what is going on is reflected in the past. The book starts from Winston, trying to write in the privacy or lack thereof in his home at writing desk, hidden from view of television on a diary, and we see our see our first glimpse of what’s wrong with this world - writing is no longer encouraged and instead, everything is dictated, making it much easier again to monitor people or what they’re saying. Similarly, English is simplified to "newspeak" to ensure words can only ever have one meaning and vocabulary is limited so words never make you think. Sex is reduced to an act done solely for procreation as your duty to the government/country but not necessarily something you'd approach outside of that - this is implied for two reasons: they want their citizens to be miserable; all that frustration can be channeled into projecting the same onto something else but also because physical intimacy implies freedom to express and to love - fundamental human experiences that the party doesn't want you to have because that is just a road away from realising the debilitating fuckedupness of your own situation. You are not allowed time away to be on your own - you go from work to communal recreational activity to home only for sleep and repeat; individualism invites space for reflection/thoughts.

Class plays an important role here as well - most of these things are only applicable to the party officials while the monitoring on proletariats is less severe, mostly restricted to propaganda that justifies their poor living conditions. People believed to be "smart" are often made an official, purely because it is easier to control them from the inside while proles are believed to be too ignorant to rebel - these freedoms are allowed for them as distractions to keep the content. Rewriting history helps because nothing can ever be proven otherwise making it difficult to incite reasonable doubt for a riot.

"If both the past and the external world exist only in the mind and if the mind itself is controllable when then?"

In Part 2, Winston performs his singular act of rebellion by getting into a relationship with Julia - we seem them reclaim their own humanity and agency with this affair (I loved it for them). We also get some excellent commentary via Julia of apathetic activists who themselves are in a better off condition than the thing they're against - she is someone who only pushes back when directly affected. Orwell seems to use her to critique a certain kind of political apathy: the person who grumbles about injustice but doesn't engage in systemic resistance.

Winston believes that while the Party can control actions and thoughts outwardly, it can’t reach the core of a person’s self - their private feelings and loyalties. This line of thought is ultimately challenged and demolished presenting the ultimate truth - human spirit is not immovable when alone (hence the isolation during torture) and can be broken down until you're a shell of a person you were, looking onto your torturer as also your savior ultimately letting yourself be brainwashed.

While the monologue dedicated to breaking down the 3 slogans of the Party definitely dragged on and suspended into a full blown Orwell rant, the critique Orwell makes throughout of class structure and. power as a form of control is still relevant. In earlier times, inequality was explained as a necessary evil for the greater good. But in Oceania, the Party no longer pretends that inequality serves a higher purpose.

Big Brother is employed as a farce by the Party as sort of a mythical figure that inspires fear & loyalty, it is much easier to worship a singular person than an entire group of people behind it, this allows people to project onto him an image of who they want him to be (parasocial relationships). He becomes whatever the people want him to be to worship him.

We are also left debating if Winston in love with Julia - it feels like he knows things logically but doesn't feel them since he has eroded away all human emotions as a byproduct of working for the party. In Part 3, the downfall (& all hope I had for a revolution fades) as Winston faces torture. While not the ideal hero-saves-the-world story, this is the more realistic route since a singular person cannot overthrow a totalitarianism society - there can be no one hero.

Aug.review:
3.5/3.75

This was an incredibly entertaining book, let’s get that out of the way. It took inspiration from the mysteries of yesteryear, most notably Agatha Christie and it delivered a product that was so incredibly unserious yet entertaining.

I have come to realise that with Riley Sagar, it’s always either hit or miss and sometimes even when it’s a hit, it’s really a miss, but I ignore it because his books are all so fast pacedso somethings always happening.

The main character, Anna, is genuinely making the worst decisions at every single turn. She spends ALL her money on this train journey to gather all these criminals that have killed hundreds of people in the past, and she determined to let them all suffer with no concrete plan as to how and she is so surprised when one of these criminals does something egregious. Fork found in the kitchen much? What works here is that Anna is very much like an average person. She is not shown even in her past to have any deal capabilities that would differentiate her from other people, and we see her solely driven by sorrow, and urge to take revenge on these people that have ruined her life.

The killer was so incredibly obvious from the get go. We knew who it was like you had to have known that if a character pops out out of nowhere in the book and is revealed to be the mysterious seventh person, and all of these murders are happening in between who do you think it is?

The way you approach this book is to just turn off your brain and have a good time because the instant you start thinking too much about everything and how things lineup so coincidentally you won’t have a good time. It’s completely unserious and I refuse to look at it any other way which contributed to the rating.

What did however bring the reading down is how terrible the writing is. I understand that you are taking a very cliche concept and you were trying to do something that honours it while bringing something to the table, but why did it read like Riley had roots in wattpad? there were so many instances where the book did not read like a book, but a parody of what they think a book should be like, and what a character should be feeling.

Aug.title: Inspector Imanishi Investigates
Aug.author: Seichō Matsumoto
Aug.review:
4.5

This was a mystery/crime fiction unlike any I've ever read which is a tall claim. The timelines felt incredibly realistic and the investigation slogs on over months which feels very true to a police procedural. 1960s Japan is a timeframe I had no idea of but Matsumoto was able to paint a picture of it so thoroughly via Imanishi's travels - we start in the developing metropolitan city of Tokyo contrasted by rural areas in decline, cities like Osaka and Kyoto rebuilding themselves post war.

Matsumoto Seicho’s Inspector Imanishi Investigates is a page-turner which picks up around the 50% mark. The narrative switches between Imanishi's investigation alongside the young Yoshimura who are quickly closing in on the facts of the investigation and beginning to ask uncomfortable questions about the men that make up the Nouveau Group. The pace is fast and the complexity of the plot leavs you hanging for more. This is contrasted by glimpses of Imanishi's life aided by scenes from his home life (his wife is a saint), his special interests (bonsai and haiku) and lush descriptions of the places he sees during his official and unofficial trips.

This mystery was a perfect "slice of life" mystery for me in a way we don't see anymore - more often than not, all mysteries seem to increasingly be categorised into "cozy" or "thrillers". Inspector Imanishi Investigates steps outsides these genre confining boxes defining its own niche with a police procedural fit for an early 2000s detective show.

Matsumoto does an excellent job of misleading his readers and for once, I was totally fooled - I had fallen into the red herring he laid out.

Aug.title: Careless People: A Cautionary Tale of Power, Greed, and Lost Idealism
Aug.author: Sarah Wynn-Williams
Aug.review:
Just like my rating (3.5), I lie somewhere in the middle of all of the gushing and damning reviews this book has received.

It is incredibly important to acknowledge the meteoric rise of technological companies that aim to both influence user purchasing patterns, opinions and also sell the same to third parties for their own undisclosed use. The understanding of technology offered as a product is largely limited to "allowing users to connect and communicate" or "purchase goods" but in the recent years, it has become clearer and clearer that data privacy is a bigger concern - nothing is truly erased off of the internet and we need to be more cognisant of the sites we engage with. Everything we do is "tracked" to optimise engagement and have the product be "addictive" by nature. While that is a concerning pattern, we also need to acknowledge the other elephant in the room : lobbying. A lot of technological companies lobby governments for their own political reasons to forward their own business. At the end of the day, we are consumers and the apps we use are maximising profit, by hook or crook. Often times, such things are not obvious or transparent and we often forget about it, I know I do.

This book is incredibly important with respect to urging readers to acknowledge the reality we live in and the role technology plays in every aspect of our global proceedings right now. It is a call to be more aware as consumers and ultimately, highlights the lack of regulations and how much we still don't understand about technology especially with rapidly increasing technological advancements.

With that being said, the author is an incredibly frustrating narrator - the book suffers from lack of editing with chapters on & on drawling about the same points. In her early days at Facebook, she struggles with saying no and feels liberated when her husband helps her cope with the same but what she struggles with are inane requests ANYONE should be able to say no to. At the same time, it's difficult to ignore her own role in all of this - her work speaks less of one that does policymaking and more so seems to focus on building political relationships with governments around the world to ultimately "sell" Facebook as a service. That does not feel like policymaking to me. I respect her for the courage to throw her NDA in the water and reveal not only the external but internal decision making aspects of Facebook. However, Sarah never seems to realise she is also a Careless Person and just as complicit in the instances she reproaches her colleagues for - the only difference is she got out and chose to speak about it.

May.title: Tell Me What You Did
May.author: Carter   Wilson
May.review:
This very much fulfilled what it set out to do. As a thriller, Tell Me What You Did fulfilled exactly the highs of the genre.

The premise was honestly very unique to me. I love the idea of a podcast which typically involves mixed media this book managed incorporate to all of those elements very well. I especially loved the links of video recordings presented as evidence in between the book - that added another layer to it. The mystery in itself was very interesting - at the core of this book what we are really exploring is whether the killer is who he says is. If you go one level deeper, it’s also about whether we should be taking matters into our own hands and what to do when the system fails you.


With all of that being said is why I give this book 3 star rating because it managed to keep me engaged and rushing through the audiobook and the e-book in three days straight. I would’ve liked to see more of would be the momentum that we had in the first 30% of the book - that was incredibly fast paced and kept me at the edge of my seat honestly, but the more we got into the second half of the more things slowed down and honestly felt like they were repeating at some point - we were having largely the same conversations with different people and exploring different perspectives of what Poe had done from people in life. I would’ve also liked it if we had maybe explored a bit more about Hindley and about who he was just to freshen things up a little and not rehash over Poe’s life story so much.

Maybe an anonymous perspective of the killer where we don’t know whose perspective are we getting would have been fun and sort of contributed to the main theory - I feel at about 70% I was able to start putting things together which feels like a mystery well executed. Lastly, I loved that while Poe was drunk for most of the book, but we still didn’t have the unreliable narrator which is an overdone trope at this point

Jul.title: Remarkably Bright Creatures
Jul.author: Shelby Van Pelt
Jul.review:
Remarkably Bright Creatures is a book that has been on my radar for a while - everyone around me seemed to love it but something about the cover dissuaded me. Goodreads has started a reading challenge where you collect bookmarks via fulfilling criteria for each of those bookmarks – I understand it for what it is but it's fun nonetheless and it prompted me to read this book.

My expectations and understanding about RBC was way off - I went in to this, thinking it's a plot-filled book with a mystery at its core (Eric somehow is alive was my best guess) and it completely flipped all of that on its head.

Very slight spoilers
The book very quickly establishes a couple of things -
1. Eric is very much dead.
2. We follow two characters (Tova and Cameron) who live in completely different states with starkly different lives but it is consistently implied that their lives are tangled in some way.
3. Marcellus can speak but he is also nearing his full age as an octopus.

In a way, there is no mystery to be discovered because the book presents most of its facts upfront and the rest of it feels very obvious but the charm is hidden, not in the plot (of which there is arguably little of) but the vibes

Tova's sections were my favorite - her character has a lot more depth and being in her head established the setting so much better for me. Her lived experiences, emotions and thoughts felt so authentic to her character and her approach to life genuinely made me smile. I loved all the people she had in her life and the way they approached their friendships and relations to other people - it made me hopeful for an old age where I foster similar friendships. It was incredibly tender to read about and moved me to tears multiple times - her pain was very real and so was her happiness at all the obscure little things in her life.

When Janice said - "That's your problem, assuming it's a burden", it felt such a throwaway way of saying a lot in very little. Tova lives her life, isolated from others, afraid to let her guard down over the sorrow she still feels with the death of her son and husband. She presents herself as someone fiercely independent and steely but it's so reassuring to know that there are people who still look out for her, who don't consider her a burden and who go out of their way to "trouble" themselves for her.

Marcellus had me immediately captivated - he had astute observations about humans and like seemingly everyone else that read this book, I researched about Pacific Octopuses and became fascinated about all that the sea hides from us in plain sight. He was both funny and serious at the same time and his entire journey, though sparse, made my heart soar.

Cameron was meh - he was okay to read about and he definitely has a character development for the better in our book version of Stars Hollow but boy, was he insufferable and entitled at the big age of 30. He blamed everyone else for the way his life turned out, felt he was entitled to his dues despite so many having it so much worse and also the constant objectification of his to-be love interest felt really weird and out-of-place in the book tonally.

Jun.review:
4.5

Okay, so truth be told, I always check the reviews first before writing a review for creative inspiration and mostly because I often forget the nitty gritty of what I read a month post reading it - this book seems to be super polarising, I saw so many extremes which, in hindsight, does not surprise me.

Thankfully, I had a great experience reading this - I often view romances with a side eye because more often than not, romances don't work out for xyz reasons but often, at least once in a year, I try to find a romance I genuinely love. This book was one that I approached with that mindset but it was so much more than just a romance - tagging it as a romance would be discounting what it did with the rest of its cast. I truly enjoyed the premise of it; that is a major reason I picked it up - I love Office Gossip and the idea of knowing everything everyone is saying was so satisfying

but I loved how feel-goody this was in terms of -
1. Find out what everyone is saying about you.
2. Get mad and convince yourself this reaffirms your own beliefs about everyone else.
3. Come up with a plan to be better at your job because you can't afford to get laid off
4. Shocker, you spend more time with your colleagues and learn they're real people.

I loved the relationships that Jolene forms with people in her team, the office idiosyncrasies and cheered Jolene for the plan she came up with at the big meeting and I especially loved her dynamic with Cliff.

I remember texting my boyfriend that the relationship between Cliff and Jolene was such a slowburn - they only kiss once and you feel so frustrated right alongside them but I enjoyed reading about two adults who acted like adults. Often times in romances even with a couple in their 30s, the text reads so unbelievable - they abandon all their responsibilities and slip into a life of just their partner (seven days in june, I am looking at you) while with this, the characters felt really grounded who were trying to address their attraction while still having an active life outside of it. I found Cliff a very fun character to read about; we don't spend too much time on how attractive he is and the author spends a lot of time fleshing out his personality and giving us enough time between Jolene and Cliff to feel the tension in how they interact + their compatibility. All of this made their relationship so much fun to read about.

I would say, I didn't care much for the arc with Armin - it felt too long and stretched on forever but I enjoyed the look it gave into Parsi families (very similar to desi families, who would've thought?)

Jun.title: Harrison Bergeron
Jun.author: Kurt Vonnegut Jr.
Jun.review:
This was such an interesting short story - every single time I read a book from Kurt Vonnegut, I am struck by the impossibility of how accurately he imagined the modern landscape of a world he'd never live to see.

This story was a little odd in terms of the 14 year old and the empress he chose but overall, without delving into semantics and specifics, this acutely reminded me of the time 2 months ago when the ghibli trend from AI generated images took over the internet. Ethical implications of commodifying a painstakingly hand drawn franchise aside, a lot of people took to the internet to talk about how art deserves to be accessible and they deserve to be able to enjoy art and "draw" what they would like - the concepts in this story struck me oddly similar to that sentiment i.e. People should be equal regardless of whether they have put in the effort or not to build their expertise on that skill. Kurt Vonnegut had dreamed of a world where we would be provided impediments by the government to level the playing field - the world we live in achieves the same but by providing us enablers to move further ahead than we ordinarily would have. Why do we believe in our existence being of utmost importance that it entitles us to access things we've never worked for? "Art should be accessible" - tools to create art traditionally should be accessible but tools to generate art copying distinctive art styles of individuals who've spent years honing their craft shouldn't even exist, let alone be accessible.

I also love how clouded in mystery Harrison is - the entire book seems to be hinting at Harrison sort of saving the world and overthrowing the government to free people of the shackles that hold them back but Kurt turns this on its head by making Harrison just as bad of an evil who is ready to create a ruling class and establish a hierarchy for those who get to be freed of their impediments vs who don't which, while directly opposing egalitarianism, is still not the answer

Apr.title: The House of My Mother: A Daughter's Quest for Freedom
Apr.author: Shari Franke
Apr.review:
(don’t necessarily rate memoirs and the 4 stars is not a reflection of how much i enjoyed the memoir but moreso an admiration for sharing her story & taking her power back)

to read about everything in this book made my skin crawl - there is only so much a human can tolerate in their lifetime, and these kids have tolerated and seen so much more than kids should ever have to see. this book serves as a good reminder in times like these about the dangers of commodifying your child’s life where we are seeing products of family vlogging finally turn into adults who can talk about their story.

Parents vying to be influencers need to do a better job of protecting their kids and not using farming their kids lives for content. The story of 8Passengers goes further beyond that tho; Ruby Franke is a product of her childhood & unresolved trauma further amplified by her life partner who chose to stay blind to everything that was happening and Jodi, who aided in the absolute destruction of the family in guise of therapy.

It is almost terrifying to see the levels to which Ruby was already exhibiting science of physical abuse alongside emotional even when her eldest were at a young age and the worst part is that reading excerpts from when Ruby was a YouTuber, despite not having seen their content before, as a normal viewer, I bet I could not have even figured that something was amis, with what Ruby was saying re her parenting ideologies which makes it worse because child abuse becomes that much harder to detect.


Reading parts where Jodi was introduced was especially painful seeing the level of gaslighting, and self doubt that she was integrating into the lives of everyone who were in vulnerable positions looking to better themselves and trusted her with their feelings. The part where Shari speaks about how Jodi is truly masterful at what she does; how we think we would he immune to it until we actually encounter about is a tale in caution about not letting yourself fall into an echo chamber to protect yourself from cults especially those guised under wellness.


To end with, I hope that the author and all the kids involved are able to process the lifetime trauma and move forward untangling the deeply ingrained thought process of denigration from their mindset. I hope the author is also able to recognise the role their own echo chamber of a community played in perpetuating the beliefs that ultimately turned on this family.

Ultimately, this is a commentary on how our system continues to fail us - How can multiple reports to the CPS go unnoticed and be dismissed due to the lack of evidence? Child abuse is not always visible and the system needs to do a better job of protecting children who are the most vulnerable to abuse under the hands of their parents.

Apr.title: The Truth of the Aleke (Forever Desert, #2)
Apr.author: Moses Ose Utomi
Apr.review:
4.5

this book was quite literally unputdownable. I started it off, thinking I would read 30 pages or so and go to sleep but I ended up reading the entire thing in one go. a testimony to the world that the author has created with the forever desert trilogy. My experience with the story of Osi was incredibly enjoyable - even moreso than the first one. Due to the established world, the author was able to pack this novella with a lot more plot and events in comparison to the first. The lore we do have in this book is all interspersed as part of the plot told in bits and pieces.

I enjoyed the callback to the story of Tutu and the way, the author crafted that story to transform with the upcoming generations, showing how histories often rewritten by those in power to support their own agendas, and cannot be trusted at face value. The people of the City of Truth have made the downfall of Tutu as the governing principle of their life, living in constant fear of the cult of the aleke - never once questioning the figure or how the increased taxes have not led to any more safety than before.

Moses is not afraid for his characters to be broken not just in spirit but also in body - this is particularly new for me in fiction wherein typical fantasies will have the main characters incur war with no real serious injuries or blemishes to their body. With the injuries that are character sustain, it increases the stakes a lot more and brings to reality the fact that at the ground level of every war are citizens who have been fed a doctrine from a very young age and sacrifice their lives while the ones in power sit comfortably watching it all unfold and having it all play out for them.


The only place where the book fell flat for me, was the ending, which kind of came out of left field. I can understand the shock value that it brings to the book and how it turns the situation on the reader who think they can predict the ending. But due to the lack of any thing that would hint at it, it truly felt like it was only placed due to the shock value. My only redemption with the ending would be the fact that we know that the suppose bad guys are the ones who hold the truth & every war starts off with two sides, both of whom think they are right.

Lastly, I enjoyed Osi as a character I enjoyed how he was and how he had a lot of growing up to do just like tutu - he believed in a very idealistic view point of the world where things are right and wrong implicitly but sometimes that’s not the case, and he does go on to learn that the world does run in many shades of grey

Apr.title: The Lies of the Ajungo (Forever Desert, #1)
Apr.author: Moses Ose Utomi
Apr.review:
4

Do yourself a favor and read this book. With a page count of under 100, 'The Lies of the Ajungo' took me by surprise with a masterclass in creating an intricate mystery, satisfying world building and a fable at its heart. It is in and of its own a feat to write a complete story within this page count and Moses Ose demonstrates the same so brilliantly in this novella - the author manages to pack in action, adventure and twists - truly displaying that you don't need a 350 page count for an immersive experience.

My expectation with this book was of a young boy going out into the desert, honing his skills, meeting friends along the way & the ultimate showdown with the root of evil ('Ajungo') bringing glory to his people and while all of that did happen, it materialised in an entirely unexpected manner. The core of this story lies in forcing the readers to question their biases, what we interpret when presented with a situation and ultimately how nothing is as it seems.

Every word in this book is so intentional, each character and their place in the story is so important inching Tutu and the reader to the truth with just the right amount of foreshadowing.

|| SPOILERS ||
If I were to analyse this book, in a way, the mechanisms employed here mirror the real world - promoting infighting between people, atrocities performed in the name of a greater evil that no one has ever seen & the clear class divide between the rich & the poor - it's not difficult to see the motivation behind the book. Our world today is not too different from the one in The Lies of the Ajungo - we go through our lives paying our own 'tax' in exchange for 'water' albeit the water itself may be meagre or just enough for us to not complain, we live in the shadows of the ones in power who makes these decisions on our behalf and we fight amongst ourselves to prevent unifying against real evil.

Jan.title: Fahrenheit 451
Jan.author: Ray Bradbury
Jan.review:
revised rating to 4.5(1)

Fahrenheit 451 took me for a ride with its beginnings so disappointing I practically abandoned the book for 2ish months and only the flurry of the news in US right now + a youtube video motivated me to start it again. Luckily, the book turns around and honestly was a delightful reading experience.

I had the displeasure of learning Branbury's intentions when writing F451 - primarily written to boo critics who had pointed out the racist/sexist & xenophobic text in is prior book and believing the outrage was indicative of a future of censorship where nothing polarising could be written without it offending someone.

I don't agree with Branbury's motivation and choose to view F451 in isolation of his own views because of how important the text is with respect to current times. I feel so strongly about the future he envisioned coming to life for the wrong reasons - we live in a time of depleted media literacy, a time where AI influencers are very rampant and ragebait is continually used as as a tool of capitalistic brands to farm engagement for their brands. We do live in a world where books are targeted by hostile governments - you cannot control a book or the intentions an author may communicate in his text and ultimately the personal interpretation the audience takes away from it and ultimately, we want to replace all of that with media that can be much more easily controlled.

This isn't just limited to book banning but the simplification/rampant summaries of books, we'd rather SparkNotes/ChatGPT our classics than actively engage with the material of our book. Popular influencers who've built their platforms on reading complain about having to read paragraphs. W
Between the book-burning and discouragement of education and learning, we’re well on our way to creating a reality way too similar to the world of the book. F451 plays with a lot of themes - we often only associate censorship with the book however, themes explored in relation to social media (TV), the need for people to move on from one thing to another with no real reflection and how quick gratification ruins literacy/thinking is incredibly relevant on a more personal level across people.

Bradbury has a quote which encapsulates it best - censorship didn't affect the society, they stopped reading of their own accord (presumably moving to better mediums such as TV/summaries)

We are at as much of a danger from censorship from the government as we are to the dangers of falling prey to trends of brain rotting and doomscrolling, refusing to be intellectually challenged by the media we consume day in and out, boxing ourselves into our comfortable echo chambers with the sameness of our opinion everywhere. We are the danger to books as much as the looming threat of banned books.

May.title: How to Write a Love Story
May.author: Catherine  Walsh
May.review:
3.5 stars! Read till 70% (yes sacrilegious I know)

I stopped at 70% because I’ve gotten everything I could have gotten out of the book and didn’t want to go in foe the third act - I really enjoyed this and where I stopped is not indicative of that. My track record with romance is the road not taken, I barely read it and when I do, I either DNF it or it’s a favourite but I am happy to have found myself a middle-of-the-road read. How To Write A Love Story is so readable, I read 40% of it in one go - I am a sucker for books within books & a big-town mc having to go into a small-town & realising the beauty of it is SO good. The characters, Sam & Ciara, were so fun to read from the view of - I rarely read male POVs but this was done really well & earnestly. Him being a fanboy & how his life’s trajectory was decided by Ravian was done really well - it felt authentic & genuine. Ciara, on the other hand, as the struggling daughter living upto her father’s legacy in the midst of her grief in a big house was every bit spontaneous & quirky ad a 2000s romcom (my favorite kind!) - she did speak a bit too young for her age but other than that, she was reallu likeable. The side characters were well fleshed-out and didn’t feel too gimmicky with at least a page or two each for their development - the whole book hinged on the community of carrigwest, it felt like a real town with people showing up for each other in good & bad. I had fun with it & would recommend to anyone looking for a summery slow-burn with lots of tension & moments.

Spoilers(!!!!) - The only reason I stopped reading is because they move to NY at the end of the book which is practice, I know, his job is there but I just couldn’t understand why’d you setup such an interesting setting just to take it away - apparently the third act involves her house getting demolished in some way which is so unnecessary and feels like plot armour to force a reason to move to NY. I know the ending would’ve pissed me off so I just stopped at the point that felt right to me

May.title: The Merge
May.author: Grace          Walker
May.review:
3.25 ⭐️

I had very high expectations for this book - the blurb spoke of a world where two minds can merge into one living on in one host body and how a mother-daughter duo are looking to merge with the latter trying to hold onto her mother for as long as possible since her mother suffers from a deteriorative dementia. The ethical questions this book posits are very interesting hinging on consent, body autonomy & how far can you push to stay with the people you love.


The book is divided in two parts - The Preparation Period & The Village. Part 1 is a dual-perspective on Laurie & Amelia as they go through the three month preparation for the merge. We are introduced to three other pairs preparing for their own merge in their cohort (a pregnant couple looking to merge presumably for the betterment of their baby, a father-daughter duo with the daughter a recovering addict, a brother duo with the older brother suffering from leukaemia) - their cohort is an experimental merge looking to solve problems that haven’t been addressed. They have a found family vibe going on, this part also sets up a lot of context about the world they live in - the protests against the merge, the government sponsored benefits for those that merge including lower taxes & increased chances of promotion. The world suffers from some degree of global warming where sunny days are the norm & rain is faint and UK is suffering from
an overpopulation issue which is where the Merge comes in, an easy way to control population by merging people. Part 2 follows Laurie-Amelie post the merge and follows the crux of the book’s reveal against the corporation.

What didn’t work for me largely was Part 2’s pacing, it was slow and dragged continuously in loops - I can imagine this works for some people but not for me. I had to really push to continue reading only for my curiosity on what happens. The big reveal is so out of left-field, it exchanges one unexplained science for another and doesn’t feel rooted in reality in context of the world - mass gaslighting much? This is a personal preference but I prefer when books stick to one side - you’re either revolutionising against the corporation or you’re not - Amelie always feels like she has one step in, one step out ultimately leading to a very bland book. I would’ve preferred if the author leaned in to the revolutionary aspect of it - at least for me, the world is already bleak as it is, I don’t want my fiction yo be the same. I had a whole nightmare about The Merge & how I wouldn’t want to lost my autonomy but the book doesn’t really sell any reasons for why people would do it out of their own choice even though that seemed to be some of the cases. Why would anyone lose their autonomy? Why would the public let the King die for e.g in the UK and not just ask the King to merge with the upcoming descendant?

I am very split about this first addition that I did. I found this book through an Instagram post about punk comics and I was really interested in the idea of technology being an all absorbing force. I feel like that is quite relevant to the world today and I want to read an artist’s take from it from almost a decade ago when things were not so dire. I enjoyed the story but I think this issue was too short for it to have been so confusing. Maybe the author’s note should have been at the start; by the time I started understanding things, the issue was already over. I also hate the obvious sexualisation of women. It’s so weird, off putting and misplaced - like oh what do you mean that the main male character hates intimacy so she’s just going to ride him in the town square, that is insane.

I think I might continue this and give it another shot for an issue or so just to see if things pick up and I am able to establish an interest in it.

Mar.title: Carrie Soto Is Back

Mar.review: I read this book in the span of 36 hours w the majority of it read on a Monday. That’s insane for me to think about - to dedicate my time deliriously to a sport I have never cared for on the dreaded start of the week. I enjoyed this book far too much; it isn’t perfect but it took me out of a slump, made me care enough about tennis to search the next upcoming Slam, I understand tennis a bit better now and I see myself looking up to Carrie Soto - I admire her determination and dedication, like it’s fucking inspiring to read about and I could use some of that in the state I am right now. I loved reading about Carrie Soto, I was cheering her on and I have loved watching her grow - in a world where women expire at the first grey hair, it is so wonderful to read about a woman who finds peace at being 37 and dreads being 17 again. The character developments and arcs, while a little cheesy, felt realistic enough for me to ignore the cringe - I am so happy Carrie has people in her corner, I am so happy she opened her heart up to let all these people in her corner. I am being super cheesy right now.

Jan.title: What the Wind Knows
Jan.author: Amy Harmon
Jan.review:
3.5 stars!

I have a lot of mixed opinions about this book - we read this for a book club and it is 100% my fault for going in blind because I thought this would be of a romance based in ireland with a woman who’s in the throes of her grief. The book is actually just that but the time travel is what I did not really expect. I loved the writing - it was so lyrical and poetic. Learning the historical references and Ireland’s history pre-partition was eyeopening.

it’s definitely a me problem but I did not really connect with any character apart from Eoin. A lot of it was just me put off by the weird dynamic of having your grandfather be your son - that was accepted too easily in the course of things but as the reader, i couldn’t separate those two identities. The romance didn’t move me very much, I loved reading about it but their separation didn’t faze me too much and the grief they held over it wasn’t in proportion to the romance we saw between them - their love for each other felt like early dating to me so I was not really able to relate to it. When I really think of it, tonally the book felt very same throughout the text to me like the grief didn’t bring forth anguish in me and similarly, nor did the other emotions.
